In recent years, technology for semi-automated ro-
torcraft of a variety of conﬁgurations has become
inexpensive enough to be considered for the educa-
tional market. These crafts range from traditional he-
licopter conﬁgurations to the now popular quad-rotor
craft (Fig. 79.7b). The key technical advances have been
in the integration of small gyros and accelerometers to
allow much of the ﬁne control to be done onboard al-
lowing the operator to worry only about the crafts’ gross
motion.
These inertial sensors have been combined by re-
searchers with precision positioning systems such as
a Vicon system to allow aerial acrobatics that rival the
capabilities of humming birds and insects [79.60, 61].
Even without the external precision positioning sys-
tems, manufacturers have been able to produce some
inexpensive platforms capable of good performance
(Fig. 79.7). The communications for some of these sys-
tems are down via standard Wiﬁpacket or via infrared
(IR) encoded commands. It is relatively easy to have
computers talk to these platforms, and as a result pack-
ages are being put together to use these vehicles to
encourage students to learn programming [79.62]. The
AR Drone has already been used in autonomous ﬂying
vehicle contests organized by KIPR (Fig. 79.7c).
It is expected that aerial robotics platforms will be-
come a major portion of educational robotics programs
in the very near future.
79.4 Education Robot Controllers and Programming Environments
Education and entertainment activities in robotics
sometimes run at cross purposes. For entertainment, we
want robots that are active, very easy to use and to con-
trol. Products like the Lego Mindstorms provide both
a robot controller and a programming environment that
meets those criteria.
However, when it comes to robot education, it is im-
portant to remember that in most cases, we are using
robots to inspire and motivate students to learn – learn
many things of which robotics is just one. Robotics
educators, especially at the K-12 level, are hoping to
teach students general science, programming, math, and
engineering techniques. The toy programming environ-
ments used in some products such as Mindstorms, may
be inappropriate for this mission.
This section overviews some of the popular robot
controllers and programming environments. Usually
the two are linked, but there are some environments that
work with several different controllers, and vice versa.
As
with
the robot tournaments described
in
Sect. 79.2, many of the robot controllers and their pro-
gramming environments in use for tournaments and by
hobbyists can trace their origins back to the MIT 6.270
course [79.32]. At an even more fundamental level, the
origin of most robot controller starts with the Motorola
68HC11 processor.
79.4.1 Robot Controllers
The venerable HC11 is a single chip processor with
small amounts of onboard ﬂash and RAM (random-
access memory). It also has a number of I/O and
timing ports that make it relatively easy to inter-
face to sensors and external devices. The 8-bit HC11
uses the same instruction set as the Motorola 6800
series of processors – which have been in exis-
tence in one form or another for more than three
decades.

Part G | 79.4
2124
Part G
Robots and Humans
Fig. 79.8 The HandyBoard with
its expansion board and the BASIC
Stamp
The HC11 was used by Anita Flynn and Joe Jones
in a board for the MIT robot talent show in 1991,
which spawned the Book Board [79.63] the MIT 6.270
board and Fred Martin’s Handyboard. The last of these
became the de-facto high-end robot controller for hob-
byists and autonomous robot contests for most of the
1990s.
The Handyboard (Fig. 79.8) can provide PWM con-
trol for four direct current (DC) motors, read 8 digital
and 8 analog sensors, control a couple of light-emitting
diodes (LEDs) and has a 32 character display. With
the expansion board, 8 lines of DIO and control for 6
RC servos is also added. The Handyboard can be pro-
grammed using 6811 assembly language and several
other languages including Java and C.
The other low-cost commercial robot controller in
wide spread use throughout the 1990s was the BASIC
Stamp [79.64] (Fig. 79.8). This PIC-based controller
could be programmed in a special (often assembly
language-like) version of the BASIC language. While
very small in memory, and usually requiring supple-
mentary electronics for most sensors and actuators, the
Stamp was very popular because of its low cost and
ﬂexibility.
In the late 1990s, spurred on in large part by the
growing interest in robot tournaments, a renaissance
in robot controller hardware started making available
a)
b)
c)
Fig.79.9a–c One of the smaller Arduinos: (a) the Digispark; (b) the Arduino Duemilanove; (c) a Shield compatible with
the Duemilanove
a number of controllers ranging from advanced PICs to
full blown PCs. Two approaches to robot controllers,
and their environments seem to be dominant in the ed-
ucation market.
The ﬁrst approach is to use a microcontroller that
is programmed using a PC and has program compiled
on the PC and then downloaded to the microcontroller
which can run that program – and little else until new
software is downloaded to it. This follows the model
originally used in 6.270 and typiﬁed by the Handy-
board but has been perfected by the Arduino family of
robot processors.
Arduino is an open source project started in 2005
in Italy [79.65]. There are more than a dozen ofﬁcial
Arduino boards available in a range of sizes and ca-
pabilities. The smaller Arduino’s are about the size of
a 1 Euro coin. Most are based on the ATMega series
of processors, but some of the newest are using ARM
processors [79.66]. Most of the Arduino boards contain
some number of digital input and output pins as well
as analog inputs and the capability to generate PWM
signals for controlling dc motors or hobby servos. Ar-
duino Shields are accessory boards that can be used to
add a variety of capabilities and ale add breadboarding
and experimental interfaces (Fig. 79.9).
In contrast to the Arduino family of controllers,
the KIPR Link [79.67], and its immediate predeces-

Robotics for Education
79.4 Education Robot Controllers and Programming Environments
2125
Part G | 79.4
sor the CBC2 [79.68, 69], represent a different style
of robot controllers. The Arduinos are inexpensive,
small, and pretty barebones. The user needs to supply
a power supply, case and often supplemental circuitry,
depending on what kinds of mechatronics are being
interfaced. Arduinos were originally targeted for the
hobbyist and robot enthusiast and indeed their primary
role in elementary and secondary education is for the
self-motivated student who uses them in their extra-
curricular projects or in kits put together by a third-
party.
The Link and the CBC2, on the other hand are
ready to use units that can be interfaced with a vari-
ety of hardware without the need of tools (Fig. 79.10).
These controllers are in fact full ﬂedged computers
running Linux, but with a GUI (graphical user inter-
face) front end and built-in touch screen allowing them
to be used as stand-alone devices, if desired. These
controllers have gigabytes of ﬂash storage and host
standard ﬁle systems. Multiple programs can be down-
loaded to the Link and the ﬁle browser can be used to
select which program to run. In fact, the programs for
these controllers are compiled and linked on the con-
troller themselves using a standard Linux tool chain.
This allows these controllers to run programs in a vari-
ety of languages, and for new languages to be added as
desired. While the CBC2 and the Link can be connected
via USB (universal serial bus) to a laptop or desktop
computer as a device, they themselves can be the host to
other USB devices including webcams. The Link uses
standard libraries such as OpenCV to process the im-
ages generated by a web cam to do object recognition,
color tracking, QR code decoding, and other standard
computer vision processing.
The Link library and touchscreen and GUI allows
the user to easily interface and explore robot sensors
and effectors in ways not previously available.

Both the Link and Arduino series of controllers
owe much of their success and capabilities to the open
source nature of both their hardware and software.

Complete schematics for the boards are available to
anyone interested as is the code for the libraries and
programming environments. There are now several pro-
ducers of Arduino compatible boards, each with their
unique capabilities. Much of the power of the Link
system comes from its ability to exploit open source
libraries such as OpenCV and also user community cre-
ated libraries and tools.
79.4.2 Educational Robotics Programming
Environments
Arduino boards are programmed using an IDE (inte-
grated development environment), based on the Pro-
cessing and Wiring IDEs [79.70, 71]. Processing was
originally developed to assist artists doing graphical
and other creative projects that required coding. The
IDE is written in Java and runs on Windows, MacOS,
and Linux platforms. The primary language for pro-
gramming Arduinos is C++ and typical programs use
two special functions setup and loop. The setup
function is used to initialize variables and ports and
the loop function is called repeatedly changing the
output state of the board based on the current sensor
inputs. This model works well for many robot applica-
tions (Fig. 79.12).
The Link robot controller is typically programmed
using the KISS programming environment. Since the
Link compiles its programs onboard, and since code can
be loaded via network or via USB drive, or even typed
in directly by connecting a keyboard to the Link, many
other options for programming environments are pos-
sible. The KISS IDE consists of an editor (Fig. 79.12
right), target selector, and a variety of simulated and
hardware targets. The editor is a general purpose lan-
guage sensitive editor that helps to highlight and format
code for the user’s choice of language (C, C++, Java,
Python, etc.). Each program can then be associated
with one or more targets such as a particular Link,
a Link simulator, or the computer running KISS. This
last target choice makes KISS a general purpose IDE
suitable for writing applications that can, with recompi-
lation, work on MacOS, Windows and Linux machines
and includes cross platform graphics, camera, and se-
rial libraries. The Link simulator (Fig. 79.13) uses the
a)
b)
Fig.79.13a,b The Link simulator running the program
shown in (Fig. 79.12b). (a) The simulator displaying the
console and sensor values. (b) The simulator showing the
motor status
same libraries as the Link itself, and so can be used
for solving syntax errors and many logic errors. Calls
to the vision routines on the Link activate the we-
bcam on the laptop running the simulator allowing
a more thorough testing of robot logic on the simu-
lator than is commonly found without running large
(and particularly novice user friendly) simulators such
as Gazebo.
Like their hardware counterparts, the Arduino and
KISS programming platforms are open source. Li-
braries, development environments, and documenta-
tion are all improved by their ever growing user
communities.

79.5 Robotic Technologies for Student Learning
2127
Part G | 79.5
79.5 Robotic Technologies for Student Learning
Exclusive, robotics-oriented
curriculum
in
formal
learning faces a formidable challenge globally: while
ICT curricula are recognized across countries as an
important twenty-ﬁrst century skill for all learners, con-
tinuing educational budget cuts have re-focused capac-
ity building across educational institutions on teachers
for the foundation subjects of mathematics and lan-
guage arts, with scant resources remaining for computer
science and even less for new directions such as educa-
tional robotics. Furthermore, a major issue of concern
in numerous countries involves achievement gaps be-
tween diverse populations, and it is arguable that highly
focused robotics courses will be particularly effective
at engaging and retaining the interest of precisely the
most precocious future engineers while failing to win
over more left-brained students, further reinforcing and
exacerbating an achievement gap through the natural
process of self-selection.
79.5.1 Cross-Disciplinary Integration
of Robotics
In combating these trends, traditional schools are recon-
sidering the role of cross-disciplinary and contextual
learning, where lessons draw upon knowledge from
multiple disciplinary specialties concurrently, teaching
lateral thinking and, ideally, motivating the disciplinary
learning process by presenting compelling pathways
through which knowledge acquired will have meaning-
ful value to a problem at hand [79.72].
A number of efforts in educational robotics concen-
trate now on this form of multidisciplinary curricula
across all ages of learners, and these new directions
are likely to be harbingers of many future, success-
ful endeavours to incorporate educational, interactive
robotics into schools in ways that pervade the educa-
tional experience rather than balkanize learning into
ever more narrow categories.
Robotics is particularly apt for integrated learning
because of its inherent diversity: robots have phys-
ical form and design considerations, computational
aspects, sensors with which real-world values can be
measured and visualized, effectors and mechanical con-
siderations and even the ability to bridge the digital
and physical worlds together. As such, robotics are an
inherently cross-disciplinary medium, and this charac-
teristic is being exploited by robotics researchers to
design and pilot such integrative curriculum. ArtBotics
is one of the many programs combining creative ex-
pression with robotics, enabling creative expression
whilst using the advanced sensor and effector technolo-
gies that make robot-building a technically rewarding
experience as well [79.73, 74]. This marriage of cre-
ativity and technology, often considered opposites in
conventional educational thinking, has the potential
to attract and encourage talent from both commu-
nities by demonstrating to artists how their creative
energy can yield notable success in technology in-
vention, and by showing technically minded students
that their invention process can be as creative as it is
rational.
Arts & Bots combines craft-based robot building
with materials that are familiar to middle school stu-
dents with a USB-driven robot control board that en-
ables choreography of a physically built robotic puppet
using an iconic programming language with appropri-
ate computational complexity for sophisticated middle
school coursework [79.75]. This program has demon-
strated cross-curricular success in the sciences, for in-
stance, enabling learners in an Anatomy course to build
an elastic-band based arm model that can demonstrate
the major degrees of freedom of the human arm using
servomotors and sensors. The process of completely de-
signing and implementing a working anatomical arm,
in turn, both engages technically apt learners and drives
inquiry to achieve a worked-out solution [79.76] that
provides particularly valuable depth of learning both
about the minutiae of anatomical musculature and about
servomotor mechanisms.
The number of integrated robotics experiences is
expanding rapidly, and this in turn guarantees that edu-
cational robotics will be widely woven into the fabric of
general education, not by designing and implementing
new coursework, but by augmenting existing learn-
ing experiences and by attracting a greater diversity of
learners into every single discipline through the power
of more authentic engagement.
79.5.2 Robotics
for Computational Thinking
The ability to think computationally has become rec-
ognized over the past decade as a critical twenty-
ﬁrst century skill that prepares learners to effectively
make creative and effective use of the technology that
will doubtless suffuse society for the foreseeable fu-
ture [79.77]. Computational thinking itself is a category
of comprehension that includes understanding sequen-
tiality, thresholds, systems behavior, digital values, and
the process of decision-making and action so impor-
tant in designing new ways to embed digital systems in
process, whether in virtual or real domains. Computer
programming and data visualization are two important
and well-understood areas of inquiry that practice such

Part G | 79.5
2128
Part G
Robots and Humans
forms of thinking, and so one large movement has been
to encourage the teaching of computer programming,
whether using iconic or lexical languages, as early and
as comprehensively as possible [79.78]. The languages
that have been most successful include Scratch, Al-
ice, Processing, Snap, and LabVIEW variants. All of
these languages combine aspects of iconic program-
ming with circuit semantics that can gain intuitive
traction with learners as young as six year of age, and
this has markedly increase the market opportunity for
curricula dedicated to thinking computationally [79.79–
81].
Robotics has particular value in this learning do-
main because robots have real-time action components;
sensors that behave noisily in the real world; motors
that can have nondeterministic effects; and processors
that can be programmed directly. Furthermore, all of
the most popular iconic programming languages have
recently become so openly modiﬁable by the program-
ming community that patches enabling direct program-
ming and control of educational robotics platforms is
both easy and under way. For instance, the Finch ed-
ucational robot is now programmable in 16 separate
languages, in many cases thanks to the efforts of unpaid
volunteers [79.82, 83].
Robotics are ideally suited for active engagement
around computational thinking, and as ever greater
numbers of robot platforms become programmable via
the best iconic languages in the market, it is likely
that robotics will become the most powerful experimen-
tal domain for sensing, measuring, designing behavior,
and designing computational processes from sensors to
actions.
79.5.3 Early Childhood Robotics
An important area of change today in educational
robotics and tangible interfaces is early childhood
learning, deﬁned as preprimary levels from three years
of age through kindergarten and early primary school-
ing levels appropriate for nine year old. The early
childhood experience has been changing dramatically
due to the rapid onset of interactive screen media, and
this in turn has led to major discussions on several con-
tinents about what the appropriate role might be for
interactive media in the lives of the very young. A num-
ber of educationally chartered organizations have begun
issuing signiﬁcant guidelines and rationales regarding
new media and early childhood, from the BBC in the
United Kingdom to the most recent addition, a joint
statement on digital media standards presented in the
United States by the National Association for the Edu-
cation of Young Children and the Fred Rogers Center
for Early Childhood Education [79.84].
The current discourse on new media in the class-
room concentrates on the role of interactive screen
media, implying in many cases that interactive tech-
nologies are largely limited to the screens of traditional
computers, Chrome books, and tablet-style devices. In
this context, much of the research currently opines on
the role of digital video games in learning, commenting
on the onward rush of gamiﬁcation, and its positive and
negative consequences on learning [79.85].
In contrast to this general movement, numerous re-
searchers have begun to explore the role of robotics
and interactive electronics as tangible devices that can
support the process of becoming technologically ﬂuent
rather than simply augmenting technical literacy in the
very young. The basic argument along these lines is
that teaching children to use designed applications on
a tablet can make them conﬁdent consumers of technol-
ogy artifacts, but in fact the craft-based and engineering
design-based processes of inquiry, creation, and experi-
mentation that can be strongly associated with robotics
experiences have the potential to turn children into pow-
erful, self-conﬁdent producers of technology rather than
mere consumers.
One such tangible experiment is the Children’s In-
novation Project (CIP), led by Jeremy Boyle of Clarion
University together with Melissa Butler of the Al-
legheny Traditional School District in Pittsburgh, Penn-
sylvania (www.cippgh.org). The CIP research project
concentrates, not only on the creation of new artifacts
but also on the process of deliberate exploration of tech-
nical artifacts, introducing tangible manipulatives that
have both physical form and sensor- and motor-based
behavior, together with curricular processes that priv-
ilege inquiry, repeated close examination, observation
and documentation well above the creation of a ﬁnished
artifact. The CIP trajectory even presents electronic toys
from Goodwill stores (recycled old toys) to students,
not as toys, but as containers of raw materials. Five year
old students learn to open the plastic toys, remove and
identify components, and then reuse these components
together with custom tangible devices to create whole
new behaviors.
New media for early childhood learning is cer-
tainly an area rife with funding and speculation al-
ready [79.86]. As the study of tangible devices for early
childhood exploration takes hold, numerous projects
such as CIP will change the relationship of educa-
tional robotics to the kindergarten classroom of the
future, turning the discourse surrounding digital media
into a conversation about interaction and exploration in
ways that bridge the digital and physical realms more
meaningfully. In turn, the students of the futures will
have a ﬂuency around technology artifacts that will be
signiﬁcantly the best prior generations.

79.6 Educational Evaluation of Robot Programs
2129
Part G | 79.6
79.6 Educational Evaluation of Robot Programs
An important aspect of assessment, beyond technical
evaluation, is educational evaluation: how does human–
robot interaction change models of learning and identi-
ties with respect to technology; and how is this done in
educationally appropriate ways? We ﬁnd several tech-
niques to be applicable during each of the following
phases of an educational project:

Design-time assessment: the creation phase of an
educational robot system

Formative evaluation: during execution of an edu-
cational robot program

Summative evaluation: following completion of an
educational program.
This section will identify relevant tools for design,
formative and summative evaluation that we borrow
from the human–computer interaction community and
the learning science community. These tools are well
suited in helping researchers measure, quantify, and
communicate how educational robots can impact learn-
ing in the classroom and, beyond the classroom, in
informal learning venues such as museums and after-
school workshops.
79.6.1 Design-Time Assessment
The ﬁeld of human–computer interaction (HCI) offers
formal and heuristic techniques for addressing inter-
faces between humans and technology [79.87]. Current
HCI practice often focuses on user-centered design,
which suggests that understanding the user and the
entire task can help us to become better designers.
One speciﬁc HCI technique, contextual inquiry and
design, is especially useful for both informal and for-
mal learning venues where robots will interact directly
with students as users. Contextual inquiry guides the
collection of background data concerning interactions
taking place before inclusion of the new, to-be-designed
robotic technology, and is often achieved through the
collection and analysis of direct interviews and obser-
vations. The process includes identifying and polling
various stakeholders in the educational environment,
from the classroom as a whole to individual educators
and mentors.
A second HCI activity, modeling, guides the cre-
ation of pictorial ﬂow diagrams that identify the most
important features of the environment in which the
robotic educational technology is to be used. Workﬂow
describes the communication necessary for the class-
room activities. Sequence identiﬁes actual sequences
of action required for various activities in the class-
room (or museum). Artifact captures the relationship
of existing tools required for activities to be performed
successfully. Finally, the physical model identiﬁes how
space is used, which can be notable in the case of the de-
sign and potential inclusion of mobile robots in spaces
that were generally not designed for them in the ﬁrst
place, like conventional labs and, even worse, regular
lecture halls.
In the tradition of learning science, one impor-
tant technique to create the best possible curriculum is
aligned design, in which both the educational curric-
ula and its matching evaluation instruments are created
simultaneously [79.88]. This design-time form of align-
ment is powerful because the student experiences and
the ways in which learning will be measured can be
suited to the classroom context and to one-another with
far better results, as compared to the incorporation of
standardized evaluation metrics as an afterthought. By
the same token, in robotics we can go even further,
aligning hardware, programming interfaces, curricu-
lum, and evaluations all at the same time, thanks to the
ever more rapid design-fabrication cycles in both the
hardware prototyping world as well as the onset rapid
software development tools. Educational robotics re-
search has already demonstrated signiﬁcant gains when
robot hardware, software, classroom curriculum, and
evaluation instruments are all designed and aligned
simultaneously to yield the best possible educational
robotics learning ecology [79.89].
Design-time assessment and joint design are prin-
cipled ways of understanding and responding to exist-
ing environments. This, in turn, facilitates design-time
judgments in regards to the best manner in which
to add a new technology, such as interactive robots,
while maximizing the chances that the technology is
a real success. But it is the continual cycle of evalua-
tions during the implementation phase, that is critical
to a positive outcome. So in summary design-time
data collection and assessment helps set the stage
and control expectations. Formative evaluations and
feedback into the continuing design process, as de-
scribed below, helps keep the engineering on a path to
success.
79.6.2 Formative and Summative
Evaluation
Traditional school-based assessments of learning, for
instance, course surveys or exam grades are useful
as coarse-resolution data collection devices. However,
these do not provide sufﬁcient detail to build mod-
els of how learning is proceeding with or in spite

Part G | 79.6
2130
Part G
Robots and Humans
of technology changes, nor how further technology
changes may improve learning. Furthermore, especially
in informal settings such as museums, school-based
assessments are even more inappropriate. In such set-
tings, signiﬁcant learning results from communication.
As groups of visitors or teams of students use and
talk about a museum exhibit or project challenge, they
construct a shared understanding of the content and
context of the challenge. There is an outstanding body
of work in the education community that focuses on
this form of conversation and learning. The follow-
ing references are excellent starting points [79.90–93].
Applying this learning strategy to educational robotics
yields wonderfully rich analyses in terms of how the
robots change conversations in the classroom and in in-
formal learning settings such as museums, clubs, and
parks [79.94].
In education learning, tools include broad evalua-
tion tools for qualitatively and quantitatively construct-
ing a model of learning across the classroom and deep,
focused tools for studying the speciﬁc communication-
oriented mechanisms of learning that may inform pat-
terns of change and exploration at the student and intra-
team level. In terms of broad tools, student surveys are
one useful data collection tool. A combination of linear,
quantitative queries (called Likert scales) coupled with
open-ended essay questions such as What is the most
important concept you learned this week? invite both
statistical analysis of raw results and thematic analysis
of self-reported challenges and successes by the stu-
dents themselves. Recorded interviews with students,
individually or in teams, provides even richer informa-
tion due to the ability to ask complex What have you
learned? questions appropriate for open-ended analy-
sis, again in terms of thematic content. A deep, focused
tool that is expensive in terms of analyst resources
but generates very useful information is the ethnogra-
phy, whereby a trained observer spends, for instance,
one week tracking all the activities of two teams in
the classroom, including conversations within the team,
among team members and other pupils, and between
the team and the course instructors and teaching assis-
tants [79.95, 96]. The ethnography is intended to detail
the learning and problem-solving process that occurs in
class on a minute-by-minute basis.
Taken as a whole, the above collected data can then
be analyzed by thematic content, for themes such as
those listed in Sect. 79.1. Statistical signiﬁcance and
correlation tests can be applied to the quantitatively de-
rived results of coding all such information to yield
information on how the frequency of learning themes
appearing in conversation increases or decreases, and
how speciﬁc themes become more reﬁned or speciﬁc in
student talk over the duration of the course.
However, assessment of the educational value of
robotics programs such as those described in Table 79.1
is often trickier than evaluating programs in more
traditional disciplines. There are widely accepted text-
books and curricula for many disciplines, but not yet
for robotics. Additionally, the different educational
robotics programs described earlier take a variety of ap-
proaches toward education.
Many programs (e.g., FIRST Lego League and
RoboCup Jr.) are large programs, but are implemented
at the local level, so the experience for students can
vary tremendously from one locale to another. The more
standardized programs (e.g., Botball and FIRST) have
different educational models. FIRST uses an inspira-
tional model where students work with professional en-
gineers. Botball follows a more traditional high school
model of education where the teachers are trained in the
techniques and principles, so that they may guide the
students at a high level, but all of the work (both design
and implementation) is done only by the students.
Because robotics can serve as an unfamiliar tool for
many students in such courses and programs, evaluation
of how this unfamiliar, and potentially rich interac-
tive tool impacts student learning and perceived interest
levels in science and technology is a common focus
of educational robotics assessment. This trend is ex-
acerbated because these programs, which involve tens
or even hundreds of thousands of students, are im-
plemented by nonproﬁt companies and volunteers that
lack speciﬁc funds and training for formal assessment.
For these reasons, formal assessment of the programs
tends to be based on student and/or teacher surveys
rather than rigorous testing, and the assessment usually
focuses on speciﬁc issues (e.g., gender issues in tech-
nology education) where assessment speciﬁc funding
may be available.
As educational robotics becomes more mainstream,
we can expect that evaluation will shift from efﬁcacy
on general enthusiasm about STEM learning to speciﬁc
learning advantages derived from such robot-inclusive
coursework for follow-on coursework in diverse disci-
plines such as biology, physics, and computer science.
An important new trend in the United States offers hope
for more broadly applicable educational robotics de-
sign. To date, very successful robotics curricula has
often been hampered in terms of scaling due to the
fact that learning standards in the US have been de-
ﬁned at the state level, making it nearly impossible to
comprehensively justify new technology curricula in
all 50 states. The new Common Core standards now
published in the US have national reach across forty
states, offering an opportunity for national consistency.
Furthermore, the new Common Core includes major
categories of learning that align exceptionally well with

Robotics for Education
References
2131
Part G | 79
project-focused, integrative learning experiences that
are well-suited to educational robotics applications,
e.g., learning precision, learning persistence, learning
innovation, data interpretation, data representation, ge-
ometric measurements, use of statistics, and qualitative
functional analysis.
79.7 Conclusions and Further Reading
This chapter has given an overview of many, but by no
means all, of the educational robot hardware and pro-
grams currently available. Websites such as robots.net
and robotevents.com attempt to maintain lists of the
rapidly evolving ﬁeld of educational robot tournaments.
Keeping track of the latest hardware and software tools
are more problematic. Some additional sources for
these topics, and others covered in this chapter include:
Robots for Kids, edited by Druin & Hendler [79.97];
Robotic Explorations, by Martin [79.98]; Where the Ac-
tion Is: Foundations of Embodied Interaction, by Dour-
ish [79.99]; Piaget’s Theory of Cognitive Development,
by Wadsworth [79.100]; and Computer as Theater, by
Laurel [79.101].

Part G | 80
80. Roboethics: Social and Ethical
Implications
Gianmarco Veruggio, Fiorella Operto, George Bekey
This chapter outlines the main developments of
roboethics 9 years after a worldwide debate on the
subject – that is, the applied ethics about ethical,
legal, and societal aspects of robotics – opened up.
Today, roboethics not only counts several thou-
sands of voices on the Web, but is the issue of
important literature relating to almost all robotics
applications, and of hundreds of rich projects,
workshops, and conferences. This increasing in-
terest and sometimes even fierce debate expresses
the perception and need of scientists, manufac-
turers, and users of professional guidelines and
ethical indications about robotics in society.
Some of the issues presented in the chap-
ter are well known to engineers, and less known
or unknown to scholars of humanities, and vice
versa. However, because the subject is transver-
sal to many disciplines, complex, articulated, and
often misrepresented, some of the fundamental
concepts relating to ethics in science and technol-
ogy are recalled and clarified.
A detailed taxonomy of sensitive areas is pre-
sented. It is based on a study of several years and
referred to by scientists and scholars, the result of
which is the Euron Roboethics Roadmap. This tax-
onomy identifies the most evident/urgent/sensitive
ethical problems in the main applicative fields of
robotics, leaving more in-depth research to further
studies.

Part G | 80
2136
Part G
Robots and Humans
The philosophical issue of the relationship between
humankind and autonomous machines appeared early
in world literature, having been developed through leg-
ends and myths. In early mythology, the ancient peoples
expressed their worries about the disrupting power of
machines over the old societies: When these artiﬁcial
creatures we have given birth to, will have learned ev-
erything from us, or understood that we are weaker than
them, will they try to dominate us?
However, for almost 250 000 years humanity has
relied on tools and machines, to increase its power
by eliminating manual labor and needless drudgery.
This factor has become one of the keys to successful
economic progress, especially since the Industrial Rev-
olution and the emergence of a mechanized economy,
and even more so with the introduction of computers
and automatic machines in the twentieth century [80.1].
Today, progress in the ﬁelds of computer science and
telecommunications allows us to endow machines with
enough intelligence so that they can act autonomously.
The twenty-ﬁrst century humanity will coexist with the
ﬁrst alien intelligence we have ever come into contact
with – robots.
In a few years from now, many more ﬁelds of ap-
plication will be robotized, because robotics will have
occupied more territories. The 2013 McKinsey Report
on the ﬁve disruptive technologies, Advances that will
transform life, business, and the global economy, out-
lines advanced robotics as one of them.
Actually, we are confronted with the rapid devel-
opment of research and applications in the service
(professional and personal) robotics sector, marking the
end of the robot segregation era. The ﬁeld of social
robots – although it does not yet show dramatic sale
ﬁgures – now offers standardized market products for
consumers. We can foresee that research and appli-
cation will point in this direction, driven both by the
market demand and by the challenges and richness of
technological and scientiﬁc issues posed to the roboti-
cist researchers by the human robotics interface. Our
graying societies are open to – and demand – depend-
able and safe automatic autonomous machines to be
employed in human cooperation and assistance.
Differently from the nineteenth century – when
the novel Frankenstein appeared – today, the love and
fear, pros and cons about robots are more grounded
in science, technology, and in humanities. Along with
other applied ethics (bioethics, computer ethics) ethi-
cal, legal, and societal aspect of robotics are debated in
roboethics.
A worldwide debate on roboethics opened up 10
years ago, following the First International Symposium
on Roboethics in 2004 [80.2]. Before that conference,
the word roboethics did not exist, not in any encyclope-
dia, nor on the Web. Today, it counts several thousands
of voices on the Web, an important literature relating to
almost every robotics application, and hundreds of rich
projects, workshops, and conferences. This increasing
interest and sometimes even ﬁerce debate expresses the
perception and need of scientists, manufacturers, and
users of professional guidelines and ethical indications
about robotics in society.
Some major segments of our lives are already of-
ten dependent on sophisticated machines. However, in
some critical instances (where robots are entrusted with
human lives, such as in medicine, in human care, or in
war theaters) we are approaching an ethical and regu-
latory gap, primarily due to the lack of legal guidelines
to ascribe responsibility to software agents and learning
machines. This lack of standards and ethical rules is re-
lated to the speciﬁcity of robot and robotics, and to all
learning machines. That is, machines endowed with the
learning capacity.
The recent thrust in research and applications pro-
grams aiming towards developing robots that are able
to co-operate with humans – that is, software agents
and robots entrusted with high learning and decision-
making functions – presents many theoretical and prac-
tical cases in which moral and legal aspects of the
responsibility attribution problem for learning robots
may soon become an urgent issue [80.3].
Facing the development of ever more powerful
computers and the variety of humanoid robots, some
scholars and scientists have warned about the dangers
of the unlimited use of technology, and especially about
the hubristic endeavor to design and manufacture intel-
ligent creatures [80.4, 5].
Their concern has been ampliﬁed by the harsh dis-
cussion around bioengineering and bioethics. Less dra-
matically, others have pointed out the need to introduce
ethical rules in technological applications, especially
regarding the behavior of intelligent machines. In this
frame, the most matter-of-fact issue is: What will the
cultural and social implication of the robotics invasion
be? Could robots be dangerous to humankind in any
way?

Roboethics: Social and Ethical Implications
80.1 A Methodological Note
2137
Part G | 80.1
80.1 A Methodological Note
This chapter is of a somewhat different nature from –
although complementary to – the totality of the book,
because it deals not only with the scientiﬁc and tech-
nological issues inherent in the matter, but also with
cultural and moral topics related to the introduction of
robots in sensitive human areas.
It is an acknowledged feeling that robotics stimu-
lates some of humanity’s most fundamental questions.
This means that we shall not expect that some simple
answers be conclusive. The undertaking of discover-
ing the essence and origin of human intelligence and
self-consciousness is as tough and troubling as the chal-
lenge around the uniﬁcation of physical forces, or the
research on the origin of the universe. Simplistic an-
swers could lead to gross mistakes and we cannot obtain
correct answers if we pose the wrong questions. The
problem is that robots are machines that are more sim-
ilar to humans than anything we have ever built, and
this makes it easier, on one hand, to adopt human ter-
minology for machines and, on the other hand, to use
machine terminology for humans. This said, the authors
feel it necessary to state the following methodological
premises:

This Handbook – and in particular the present
chapter – will be read by roboticists and also by
non-roboticists, and by students of robotics as well
as by students and scholars of ethics, the philoso-
phy of science, sociology, laws, etc. Some of the
issues presented here are well known to some and
less known or unknown to others, and vice versa.
Nonetheless, the authors deem it useful and impor-
tant to recall and clarify some of the fundamental
concepts relating ethics in science and technology,
because the subject is complex, articulated, and of-
ten misrepresented.

Roboethics is an applied ethics that refers to studies
and works done in the ﬁeld of science and ethics
(S&TS – science and technology studies, science
and technology and public policy, professional ap-
plied ethics), and whose main premises are derived
from these studies. In fact, roboethics was not born
without parents, but it derives its principles from the
global guidelines of the universally adopted applied
ethics. This is the reason that a relatively substan-
tial part of this chapter is devoted to this matter,
before a speciﬁc discussion of sensitive areas of
roboethics.

Many of the issues of roboethics are already covered
by applied ethics such as computer ethics, bioethics,
or neuroethics. For instance, problems – arising
in roboethics – of dependability; of technologi-
cal addiction; of digital divide; of the preservation
of human identity and integrity; the applications
of precautionary principle; of economic and social
discrimination; and of the artiﬁcial system auton-
omy and accountability. As well as issues related
to responsibilities for (possibly unintended) war-
fare applications; the nature and impact of human–
machine cognitive and affective bonds on individu-
als and society; all these issues have already been
matters of investigation by the computer ethics and
bioethics.
Here, the speciﬁcity of robotics was underlined
from a general point of view. Subsequently, in the
taxonomy, the speciﬁc ethical issues related solely to
robotics are carefully evaluated. The present taxonomy
was not developed on the basis of the afﬁnity of the
techno-scientiﬁc or disciplinary areas – like the Index of
the present book. In the roboethics taxonomy, the grid is
based on the afﬁnity of the application of robots, and on
the speciﬁcity inherent in the human–robot interaction
of these applications.
In terms of scope, we have taken into considera-
tion – from the point of view of the ethical issues con-
nected to robotics – a temporal range of two decades,
in which frame we could reasonably locate and infer –
on the basis of the current state-of-the-art in robotics –
certain foreseeable developments in the ﬁeld.
For this reason, we consider premature – and have
only hinted at – problems related to the possible emer-
gence of human qualities in robots: consciousness, free
will, self-consciousness, and sense of dignity, emotions,
and so on. Consequently, this is why we have not ex-
amined problems – debated in some other papers and
essays – like the proposal to not behave with robots like
with slaves, or the need to guarantee them the same re-
spect, rights, and dignity we owe to human workers.
Likewise, and for the same reasons, the target of
roboethics is not the robot and its artiﬁcial ethics, but
the human ethics of the robots’ designers, manufactur-
ers, and users.
Although informed about the issues presented in
some papers on the need and possibility to attribute
moral values to robots’ decisions and about the chance
that in the future robots might be moral entities like – if
not more than– human beings, the authors have chosen
to examine the ethical issues of the human beings in-
volved in the design, manufacturing, and use of robots.
We felt that problems like those connected to the
application of robotics within the military and the pos-
sible use of military robots against some populations
not provided with this sophisticated technology, as

Part G | 80.3
2138
Part G
Robots and Humans
well as problems of terrorism in robotics and prob-
lems connected with biorobotics, implantations, and
augmentation, were pressing and serious enough to
deserve a focused and tailor-made investigation. It is ab-
solutely clear that without a deep rooting of roboethics
in society, the premises for the implementation of an
artiﬁcial ethics in the robots’ control systems will be
missing.
80.2 Specificity of Robotics
Robotics is a discipline originating from:

Mechanics

Automation

Electronics

Computer science

Cybernetics

Artiﬁcial intelligence.
However, it draws on from several other disciplines:

Physics/mathematics

Logic/linguistics

Neuroscience/psychology

Biology/physiology

Anthropology/philosophy

Art/industrial design.
Is robotics a new science?
On the one hand, robotics is often regarded only
as a branch of engineering dealing with intelligent, au-
tonomous machines. In this case, it shares experiences
with other disciplines, and it is somehow the linear sum
of all the knowledge. In fact, the keyword robotics sel-
dom appears in institutional programs, mainly being
hosted in the information and communication technol-
ogy (ICT) cluster, or hidden under different initials.
Some of us, however, see robotics potentially as
new science, in its early stage. Actually, it is the ﬁrst
time in history that humanity is approaching the chal-
lenge to develop an intelligent and autonomous entity.
This extraordinary mission gives to robotics the spe-
cial feature of being a platform where sciences and
humanities – hard and soft sciences – converge: an
experiment in itself [80.6]. Actually, it is not without
some ground that we could forecast that robotics will
emerge as a new science, with its own theory, prin-
ciples, theorems, proofs, and mathematical language.
We are just on the eve of the development of our
science. It is hard to envisage its future. It could hap-
pen that robotics will incorporate other sciences; or
that, like the giant red stars, it will explode into many
other sciences, born from the intersections of adjoining
ﬁelds.
80.3 Cultural Differences in the Acceptance of Robots
While analyzing the present and future roles of robots
in our societies, we shall be aware of the underlying
principles and paradigms which inﬂuence social groups
and single individuals in their relationship with these
machines.
Different cultures and religions regard the inter-
vention in sensitive human ﬁelds like reproduction,
neural therapies, implantations, and privacy differently.
These differences originate from the cultural speciﬁci-
ties towards the fundamental values regarding human
reproduction, life, and death.
In different cultures, ethnic groups, and religions the
very concepts of life and human life differ, ﬁrst of all
concerning the immanence or transcendence of human
life. While in some cultures women and children have
fewer rights than adult males (not even the habeas cor-
pus), in others the ethical debate ranges from the legal-
ization on a post-human status, to the rights of robots.
Thus, the different approaches in roboethics concern the
rights in diversity (gender, ethnicity, minorities) and the
deﬁnition of human freedom and animal welfare. From
these concepts all other ethical speciﬁcities such as pri-
vacy and the border between privacy and traceability of
actions are derived. Cultural differences also emerge in
the realm of natural versus artiﬁcial. Think of the at-
titude of different peoples towards surgical implants or
organ implantation; how human enhancement could be
viewed.
Bioethics has opened important discussions. How is
the integrity of the person conceived? What is the per-
ception of a human being? Last but not least, the very
concept of intelligence, human and artiﬁcial, is subject
to different interpretation. In the ﬁeld of artiﬁcial in-
telligence AI and robotics alone, there is a terrain of
dispute – let us imagine how harsh it could be outside
of the inner circle of experts.

80.4 Roboethics Foreshadowed in the Literature
Literature is the instrument by which society expresses
itself, free from rigid constraints, and by which it can
simulate future social developments. Sometimes, by
way of literature important and foresighted scientiﬁc is-
sues have been dreamt of and anticipated.
The topic of the threat posed by artiﬁcial entities de-
signed by man’s ingenuity (legends like the rebellions
of automata, the Frankenstein myth, the Golem) recurs
in classical European literature, as well as the misuse
or the evil use of the product of engineering (the myth
of Dedalus). This is not the case in all world cultures.
For instance, Japanese culture does not include such
paradigms; on the contrary, machines (and, in general,
human products) are always beneﬁcial and friendly to
humanity.
In 1942, the outstanding novelist Asimov, who
coined the word Robotics, formulated the famous
Asimov’s
three
laws
of
robotics
in
his
novel
Runaround [80.7]:
Law 1: A robot may not injure a human being, or
through inaction, allow a human being to come to
harm.
Law 2: A robot must obey the orders given to it by hu-
man beings except where such orders would conﬂict
with the ﬁrst law.
Law 3: A robot must protect its own existence as long
as such protection does not conﬂict with the ﬁrst or
second law.
Later on, in 1983, Asimov added the fourth law
(known as the zeroth law):
Law 0: No robot may harm humanity or, through inac-
tion, allow humanity to come to harm.
Over the last few decades, scientiﬁc and technolog-
ical developments have brought forward the frontiers of
robotics, so that those problems that years ago seemed
only theoretical, or a matter of literature and science
ﬁction, are becoming very practical, and even urgent.
Some of these problems have alerted the robotics com-
munity to the need to open a discussion on the princi-
ples that should inspire the design, manufacturing, and
use of robots.
Could these laws really become the ethics of robots?
Of course not. The three laws are a beautiful mes-
sage passed on to us by Asimov, but they are a literary
expression of some general principles metaphorically
applied to robotics – it is a work of art, and a source
of inspiration. However, as such these laws are inade-
quate to encompass the complexity of robotics in all its
branches and applications to society.
80.5 And Expressed in Real Robotics
In January 2004, in San Remo, Italy, the School of
Robotics, in collaboration with roboticists, philoso-
phers, and scholars of humanities, organized the First
International Symposium on Roboethics, where the
word roboethics was ofﬁcially used for the ﬁrst time
(Fig. 80.1).
In this occasion the IEEE Robotics and Automa-
tion Society established a Technical Committee (TC)
on Roboethics, with the aim of providing the IEEE
Robotics and Automation Society with a framework
for analyzing the ethical implications of robotics re-
search, by promoting the discussion among researchers,
philosophers, ethicists, and manufacturers, but also
by supporting the establishment of shared tools for
managing ethical issues in this context. The TC pro-
moted many activities, workshops, and studies on
roboethics.
In 2005, EURON (the European Robotics Research
Network) funded a project called Euron Roboethics
Atelier, with the aim of drawing the ﬁrst roboethics
roadmap. In 2006, in Genoa, Italy, scholars from hu-
manities met with engineers and roboticists for 3 days
to draw the lines of the Euron Roboethics Road-
map [80.8].
Following the First International Symposium on
Roboethics, one of the ﬁrst steps in roboethics was
to select a methodology for the identiﬁcation and
analysis of techno-ethical issues in robotics. To our
knowledge, three European projects (which also availed
themselves of international experts, as well as back-
ground studies in information and computer ethics and
in bioethics) represent the most structured efforts in this
ﬁeld. These are: the Euron Roboethics Atelier, 2006;
Ethicbots, 2006–2008; and CARE, Coordination Ac-
tion for Robotics in Europe, 2008.
As deﬁned by its designer [80.2]:
Roboethics is an applied ethics whose objective
is to develop scientiﬁc/cultural/technical tools that
can be shared by different social groups and be-
liefs. These tools aim to promote and encourage the
development of robotics for the advancement of hu-
man society and individuals, and to help preventing
its misuse against humankind.

Part G | 80.6
2140
Part G
Robots and Humans
Fig. 80.1 The roboethics’ logo, sketched by the renown
Italian artist, Emanuele Luzzati (1920–2007), is repre-
sented by a smiling young girl receiving a ﬂower from
a chivalrous humanoid robot
According to the deﬁnition, roboethics is not the ethics
of robots, nor any artiﬁcial ethics, but it is the hu-
man ethics of the robots’ designers, manufacturers, and
users.
Over the years since 2004, three different deﬁnition
of roboethics emerged, according to the epistemologi-
cal and moral conceptions of their authors. These three
deﬁnitions correspond to three different words [80.9].
The ﬁrst deﬁnition is represented by the adopted
ethical theories, developed principally by the branch of
philosophy called ethics or morality, which studies hu-
man conduct, moral assessments and the concepts of
good and evil, right and wrong, justice and injustice,
etc. In our case, a generic or fundamental ethical re-
ﬂection is directly linked to the particular issues that
are generated by the development of robotic applica-
tions and their diffusion in society. This is the proper
concept of roboethics, meaning applied ethics that, sim-
ilarly to bioethics, attempts to provide answers to new
questions that are generated by the progress of a spe-
ciﬁc scientiﬁc and technical ﬁeld. This level updates
the various views on concepts such as dignity and in-
tegrity of the person and the fundamental rights of the
individual, as well as the social, psychological, and le-
gal aspects involved. Roboethics is developed for a) the
identiﬁcation and analysis of ethical issues that arise
from current and upcoming robotics applications, and
b) the possible deﬁnition of some general guidelines on
the above. In a broader meaning of the word, roboethics
not only applies to the prohibition and/or prevention
of some actions, but identiﬁes also those trends of
robotics research and development that enhance what
are viewed as human rights (the encouragement to
some actions): robotics research and applications that
promote and enhance human rights for well-being, edu-
cation, and the right to medical care, food, housing, and
employment.
The second deﬁnition, currently referred to as robot
ethics, or machine ethics, regards the code of con-
duct that designers implement in the AI of robots.
This means a sort of artiﬁcial ethics able to guarantee
that autonomous robots will exhibit ethically acceptable
behavior in all situations in which they interact with
human beings or when their actions may have nega-
tive consequences on human beings or the environment.
It is clear that the guidelines to deﬁne what is ethi-
cally acceptable and to enforce them are the product
of the above-mentioned ﬁeld of roboethics. Robots are,
in fact, machines, meaning tools that are unaware of the
choices made by their human creators, which, therefore,
bear the moral responsibility for the actions, good or
bad, of robots.
Finally, there is a third meaning, which we could
perhaps deﬁne as robots’ ethics, because it is the ethic
born from the subjective morality of a hypothetical
robot that is equipped with a conscience and freedom
to choose its own actions on the basis of a full com-
prehension of their implications and consequences. It is
only in this case that robots may be deemed as moral
agents, and that one may refer to involving the respon-
sibilities or rights of robots. This, obviously, is currently
speculative and beyond the purposes of this handbook.
80.6 Ethics in Science and Technology
For the purposes of this study, we provide the vari-
ous meanings of the term ethics within the context of
modern debate. Traditionally, ethics is a philosophical
or theological subject that studies human behavior and
assessment criteria for human behaviors and choices.
Modern ethics have developed from various points of
view along classical philosophy. In the last decades, in
our highly complex societies characterized by techno-
scientiﬁc development, the attribution of moral and
practical responsibility is becoming more and more
difﬁcult, with regard to unintentional or collateral con-
sequences of actions and operations that are produced
by unidentiﬁable decisions (group decisions, complex
administrative structure, distribution of responsibilities,
computerized operations). Often, one ﬁnds it impossi-
ble to attribute ﬁnal responsibility to a single person

Roboethics: Social and Ethical Implications
80.6 Ethics in Science and Technology
2141
Part G | 80.6
or to a deﬁned social entity. In the absence of a def-
inition and of a precise analysis of the responsibility
chain, technologically advanced societies have shifted
the issue onto the concept of risk assessment, thereby
attributing value to the damage produced by entities that
are seemingly devoid of responsibility. In our case, the
question is: Who is responsible for any damage that
may be caused by an autonomous robot? Is it the de-
signer, the manufacturer, the programmer, or the ﬁnal
user? Often it will be difﬁcult to obtain easy answers to
this question.
From the view point of ethical theories, we observe
that individuals possess ethics of common sense, which
provide them with the moral guidelines for decision
making, from the small ones to important life decisions.
This affects day to day life, as well as our actions in
our close-knit social relations. Individuals often adopt
different ethical theories from time to time: utilitarian-
ists for some decisions, in other situations or moments
they generally go by the terms of their up-bringing, cus-
toms, tradition, and religion (descriptive ethics). And
this seems to be enough for them.
However, this line of thought reaches its limits
when, as social ﬁgures, or in our profession, we are
faced with complex problems, in which our actions may
have multiple consequences that are difﬁcult to follow
and predict; and when our common sense is faced with
problems we have never dealt with before – bioethical
dilemmas for example. In these situations, the ethics
of common sense leads to various paradoxes: we ﬁnd
ourselves without any conceptual resources and in the
difﬁcult position of having to pass judgement. In these
cases, we need a logical-critical set of ethics (critical
ethics) that: a) reveals the implicit, and perhaps never
uncovered, assumptions in our ethics of common sense,
and in our outdated ethical theoretical base; b) analyzes
reasons, the pros and cons and identiﬁes their origin.
Inevitably – we may not even realize it – we resort to
prescriptive ethics and ethical theories.
In practice, when faced with general and complex
topics, we may refer to the fundamental, relevant values
involved in our dilemmas; we may adhere to the more
updated morality applied to issues close to ours; or we
try to step up from the universally shared prescriptions
towards new ethical frontiers. Prescriptive ethical the-
ory, which develops and justiﬁes the principles of moral
actions, refers to ethical theories and the related guide-
lines. These, in turn, represent the general ideas that
contain ethical principles, in order to reach an inter-
nal and systematic coherence. In defence of the ethical
principle, the ethical philosophers either implicitly or
explicitly refer to an ethical theory.
In the twentieth century, from the dissatisfaction
raised by the issues that are deemed to be the limits
to traditional ethical theory – utilitarianism and deon-
tologism inspired by Kant – ethics became fragmented
into several forms: rights ethics, virtue ethics, feminist
ethics, and applied ethics [80.10]
According to virtue ethics – which have less to do
with single actions, but more to do with different life
styles, and ways of life – the most important moral obli-
gation is our personal relationship with or actions or
non-actions. In making or using robots, according to
virtue ethics we would analyze the effect of robots in
respect to the concept of good and happiness: Which
robots could contribute most to the happiness, to the full
and complete quality of life of human beings? [80.11]
In another instance, considering the need to account
for values that are part of a collective conscience, the
so-called rights ethics sees human rights as the most
relevant elements in common for a system of cultural
and moral pluralism, and as being reasonably deemed
to be the ﬁnal manifestation of universal ethics.
One of the challenges to traditional ethical theo-
ries by some thinkers regarded the limitation of moral
considerations to the problems of humans and of their
relationship in human society, regardless of other liv-
ing organisms and of the environment. Therefore ethical
theories, and the new applied ethical theories in partic-
ular, were called upon to include non-human entities
in their analysis (animal ethics, environmental ethics,
and planetary ethics – known as the Gaia theory), as
well as human products (bio-culture, computer ethics,
roboethics). The various ethical theories applied are,
in turn, connected and intertwined with other disci-
plines, including law, sociology (descriptive ethics),
economics, and various scientiﬁc ﬁelds.
One of the central themes of applied ethics is the
concept of responsibility, which is a moral notion. Legal
responsibility determines the rules of the relevant pre-
scriptive ethics, meaning the group of commands and
prohibitions adopted by a society or a group, and that
also deﬁnes professional ethics. For the purposes of this
chapter, to analyze the human–robot relationship, we
shall consider the two main meanings of the term re-
sponsibility:

The analysis of the identity of the agent of the cause
of certain actions and their effects (utilitarianism,
consequentialism, or teleologism)

An expression of motivations that leads an agent to
act in a certain way (deontological ethics or Kantian
ethics), according to which the individual assesses
the consequences of his or her actions.
We know that in the last century, the question What
authority and what set of moral rules am I obliged to be
accountable to? State law? God? forced many answers

Part G | 80.6
2142
Part G
Robots and Humans
(utilitarian or deontological) to a crisis point. Often, the
moral response of the individual as well as the moral
evolution of our society have led to an opposition to the
responsibility towards the nation, the church, or towards
traditional roles of social institutions (Weber’s ethics of
intentions or ethics of individual conscience) [80.12]
Some serious events related to World War Two
changed the notion of responsibility and of differen-
tiation of roles (i. e., engineers deal with engineering,
doctors with medicine, soldiers obey orders from su-
periors, etc.); and also some famous legal cases, e.g.,
the Adolf Eichmann trial, during which Eichmann de-
fended himself by stating that he was obeying orders
under his administrative responsibilities and that he did
not decide on, nor was he aware of, the entire project
of Jewish extermination; or the debate that ensued after
Hiroshima/Nagasaki in 1945.
Furthermore, there are different cases in which our
personal morals clash with those adopted and imposed
by the society we live in and whose law we live under.
Such is the case, for example, with the death penalty
(which is in force in various states in the USA, although
contested by internal currents), animal rights, abortion,
or euthanasia. In these cases, the implicit moral philos-
ophy in state laws does not coincide with the feelings
of many groups of the relevant societies, which leads to
this sort of conﬂict.
Therefore, we observe that in contemporary soci-
eties, the notion of responsibility is not limited to the
moral consideration of actions of the agent or cause, and
it does not only deal with the necessary conformity of
the action with a group of duties (therefore, the analysis
of consequences is less decisive). In today’s society, just
the elements of complexity and of technological ruling
determine the aspect that is known as heterogenesis of
ends, according to which our actions may have conse-
quences that are extremely difﬁcult to estimate, which
may even be opposite to our intentions. According to
Morin’s ecology of action [80.13], once the action de-
parts from the individual, it lives a life of its own, and
combines itself with the environmental conditions (so-
cial models, actions and reactions of other agents), and
the ﬁnal result is beyond the agent’s predictive abilities.
Faced with this vacancy in the attribution of in-
dividual responsibility, some researchers attempted to
identify collectively shared responsibilities, if impos-
sible or useless to identify individual responsibility.
In the case of scientiﬁc research, S&TS expert von
Schomberg [80.14] proposes to adopt an assessment
system based on foresight and knowledge (foresight
and knowledge assessment). The author sustains that,
because the deﬁnition of responsibility is considerably
more arduous to deﬁne in scientiﬁc ﬁelds, due to the
unintentional consequences, uncertainty, or ignorance
of results, instead of identifying the ethical responsibili-
ties post hoc, it is necessary to establish the ethics of the
overlap of knowledge between different areas before-
hand (synergy: scientists, politicians, etc.) because the
quality of knowledge shall determine the ethical value
of the applications that will follow. At the same time,
one must constantly ensure the maximum precision of
predictions in order to identify both the wholesomeness
of research and relevant applications, as well as the po-
tential ethical problems.
Other authors have emphasized the need to avoid
the overlap between ethical problems and technical so-
lutions; among the latter, the expert of computer ethics,
Mowshowitz. In his Technology as excuse for question-
able ethics he states that [80.15]:
The seemingly eternal social problems are real
enough, but to look for their cause in technique or
autonomous technology is both mistaken and harm-
ful. We should not blame technology for human
failures. (...) Autonomous technology contributes to
the belief in technological determinism, i. e., re-
inforces belief in the inability of people to make
signiﬁcant choices in their lives. It directs attention
away from wielders of power to systems of reiﬁed
collectivities. The law is smarter than the social
sciences – it deﬁnes the corporation, for example,
as a ﬁctional person for purposes of assigning re-
sponsibility and does not absolve key actors of their
responsibilities. Institutions should be seen as con-
venient ﬁctions that help explain individual decision
and action (...) Only the actions of human beings
can be alienating or dehumanizing. Reiﬁcation of
technology allows for an illegitimate transference of
responsibility from persons to a ﬁctional social con-
struct, and at the same time impedes our ability to
come to grips with the very real ethical challenges
posed by the uses of technology.
In conclusion, we observe that in roboethics, the
deﬁnition of moral responsibility, and the resulting no-
tion of liability – which is central in the human–robot
relationship – could differ according to the philosophi-
cal assumptions, which – knowingly or unknowingly –
have been adopted.
