80.7 Ethical Issues in an ICT Society
The importance of ethics in science and technology has
been demonstrated by our recent history. Three of the
front rank ﬁelds of science and technology: nuclear
physics, bioengineering, and computer science, have
already been forced to face the consequences of the ap-
plications of their research because of pressure caused
by dramatic events, or because of the concern of the
general public.
The introduction of intelligent machines in our daily
life brings up global social and ethical problems, which
are usually summarized as follows:

Dual-use technology (every technology that can be
used for civilian or military applications)

Anthropomorphization of technological products (it
is well known and documented that people attribute
intentions, goals, emotions, and personalities to
even the simplest of machines with life-like move-
ment or form)

Humanization of the human/machine relationship
(cognitive and affective bonds toward machines)

Technology addiction

Digital divide, socio-technological gap (per ages,
social layer, per world areas)

Fair access to technological resources

Effects of technology on the global distribution of
wealth and power

Environmental impact of technology.
Due to the interdisciplinarity of robotics, roboethics
shares problems and solutions with other applied ethics:
computer ethics, information ethics, bioethics, tech-
noethics, and neuroethics.
Computer Ethics (CE), is a term that was coined
by Walter Maner in the mid 1970s. It indicated the
ﬁeld of research that studies ethical problems aggra-
vated, transformed, or created by computer technol-
ogy [80.16]
Perhaps, the ﬁrst contact between ethics and com-
puter science took place in the 1940s, when Norbert
Wiener, professor at the MIT and one of the founding
fathers of computer science expressed his concern about
the social effects of the technologies he himself con-
tributed to develop. In 1948, in his book Cybernetics: or
Control and Communication in the Animal and the Ma-
chine [80.17] and successively in his other book, The
Human Use of Human Beings, he pointed out the dan-
gers of nuclear war and the role of scientists in weapons
development in 1947, shortly after Hiroshima [80.18].
Although he did not use the term computer ethics, he
laid down a comprehensive foundation for computer
ethics research and analysis. Wiener’s foundation of
computer ethics was far ahead of its time.
It was not before 1968 that Wiener’s concern be-
came actual practice, when Donn Parker, one of the
most famous scientist of SRI (Stanford Research Insti-
tute), at Menlo Park, began to examine unethical and
illegal uses of computers by computer professionals.
According to Bynum, Park then said that it seemed that
when people entered the computer center, they left their
ethics at the door [80.19].
In 1968 Parker published Rules of Ethics in In-
formation Processing [80.20], and he promoted the
development of the ﬁrst code of professional conduct
of the Association for Computing Machinery (AMC),
which was adopted by the ACM in 1973.
During the late 1960s, Joseph Weizenbaum, the
designer of the computer program Eliza, shocked by
the emotional involvement of psychiatric scholars to-
wards his simple programs, expressed his concern
that an information processing model of human be-
ings was reinforcing an already growing tendency
among scientists, and even among the general pub-
lic, to see humans as mere machines. Weizenbaum
wrote the book Computer Power and Human Rea-
son, in which expressed his thoughtful ethical philos-
ophy [80.21].
In the late 1970s, Walter Maner of the Virginia’s Old
Dominion University was the ﬁrst to employ the lemma
computer ethics to deﬁne the ﬁeld of inquiry dealing
with ethical problems aggravated, transformed, or cre-
ated by computer technology. In 1985, Moor of Dart-
mouth College published his article What is computer
ethics? [80.16] and Johnson of Rensselaer Polytechnic
Institute published her book, Computer Ethics [80.22],
the ﬁrst textbook – and for more than a decade, the
deﬁning textbook – in the ﬁeld. In 1983 at Palo Alto the
CPSR (Computer Professional for Social Responsibil-
ity) CPSR was founded. This is a global organization
promoting the responsible use of computer technol-
ogy. Incorporated in 1983 (following discussions and
organization that began in 1981), CPSR, is the ﬁrst
international association whose mission is to educate
policymakers and the public on a wide range of issues.
In 1991 computer ethics was ofﬁcially added as subject
to the programs in the computer science departments of
the United States.
Information ethics (IE) was developed in the 1990s
by several researchers (especially the Oxford team
led by Floridi), when it was proposed that the core
of the issues of CE did not lie in the speciﬁc tech-
nology, but in the raw material manipulated by it
(data/information) [80.23].
Bioethics is the study of the ethical, social, le-
gal, philosophical, and other related issues arising in

Part G | 80.8
2144
Part G
Robots and Humans
healthcare and in the biological sciences (International
Association of Bioethics, IAB).
In 1970 Van Rensselaer Potter coined the word
bioethics. He was an American biochemist, Professor
of Oncology at the McArdle Laboratory for Cancer Re-
search at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The
ﬁrst appearance of the term was in his book Bioethics,
Bridge to the Future [80.24]; he coined it after trying
for many months to ﬁnd the right words to express the
need to balance the scientiﬁc orientation of medicine
with human values.
Potter’s original concept of bioethics comprised
a global integration of biology and values designed
to guide human survival, with a new bioethics as the
bridge between science and humanities. Increasingly,
he felt the need to link what he came to realize had be-
come mainstream biomedical ethics with environmental
ethics. During his career Potter continued to modify the
term bioethics to differentiate his conceptions from the
dominant view of biomedical ethics. He eventually se-
lected the term global bioethics, and this became the
title of his second book. In it, there is a new deﬁnition
of the term bioethics [80.25]:
Biology combined with diverse humanistic knowl-
edge forging a science that sets a system of medical
and environmental priorities for acceptable sur-
vival.
The ﬁeld of bioethics is at a critical stage of evo-
lution, having now passed the 30th year of the de-
velopment of bioethics programs. It is in a phase of
professionalization attending to both the ethical frame-
work for clinical and industrial bioethical consultation
and the creation of the next level of academic organiza-
tional success, namely, departments and PhD programs.
Technoethics is a recent deﬁnition, derived from
Christian theology [80.26]:
As a sum total of ideas that bring into evidence
a system of ethical reference that justiﬁes that pro-
found dimension of technology as a central element
in the attainment of a ﬁnalized perfection of man.
Neuroethics is concerned with ethical, legal, and
social policy implications of neuroscience, and with
aspects of neuroscience research itself [80.27]. Neu-
roethics encompasses a wide array of ethical issues
emerging from different branches of clinical neuro-
science (neurology, psychiatry, psychopharmacology)
and basic neuroscience (cognitive neuroscience, affec-
tive neuroscience).
In conclusion, we can summarize the ethical issues
in advanced robotics as derived from the studies of the
applied ethics, as follows:

Under what conditions a technology is to be consid-
ered acceptable? (precautionary principle)

At what point the development of this technology is
acceptable?

How do we weigh the cost/beneﬁts ratio of an ad-
vanced technology?

How do we weigh any risk assessment?

What is the rate of the ethics of functional compen-
sation or repair vs. enhancement/augmentation?

Are there cases where a particular type of technol-
ogy itself should be considered unacceptable even
though it has potential for compensation as well as
enhancement?

The issue of identifying cause, and assigning re-
sponsibility, should some harm result from the de-
ployment of robotic technology [80.28].
80.8 Human Principles and Rights
The authors are inspired, in this study, by the thesis
of the American moral and political philosopher Rawls
and his reﬂective equilibrium [80.29]. According to
Rawls, the charters and treaties, although advanced in
an attempt to associate the highest number of partic-
ipants, and although commendable in the attempt to
widen the promotion of rights to as great a number
of members and functions as possible, do not satisfy
the possibility of positive progress, nor can they pro-
vide for the entire range of criminal uses of robots.
In roboethics, scholars are heading off to an unknown
land, where new and original solutions should be cre-
ated. However, although searching for new solutions on
its way, coherence with philosophy of law imposes that
no new form of ethics can demean the rights acquired
by the previous ones [80.30]:
Any new ethics must deal with the same substance
as the old role responsibility ethics, namely with
values and norms that restrict or delimit human ac-
tion and thus enable or guide traditional decision
making.
This statement means that roboethics and robot ethics
should be coherent with the universally shared sets of
rules.
Universal sets of rules are expressed by inter-
nationally recognized institutions such as the United

Nations, The World Health Organization, the FAO, UN-

Summit on the Information Society. Also, the European
Union has identiﬁed general ethical principles, which
have been adopted by most nations, cultures, and people
of the world. Furthermore, the international scientiﬁc,
juridical, economic, and regulatory communities have
in many occasions proposed a harmonization (univer-
sally accepted, standardized) of world ethical principles
applied to science and technology, especially in those

such as life, human reproduction, human dignity, and

For instance, the Ethics of Science and Technol-

of Science and Technology in the Social and Human
Sciences Sector, and COMEST, an advisory body to
UNESCO composed of 18 independent experts, has
proposed in the ﬁeld of bioethics to start a process to-
wards a declaration on universal norms on bioethics. In
Rio de Janeiro, December 2003, COMEST organized
an international conference on the issue of a Universal
Ethical Oath for Scientists. Because ethics in science
and technology is not limited to deontology or profes-
sional ethics, but concerns a broader range of questions
involving fundamental beliefs and moral principles, its
results and conclusions become also guidelines for con-
duct in the professional daily life.
From the social and ethical standpoint, in deciding
on the design, development, and application of a new

Computer and information ethics has developed
a code of ethics called PAPA (privacy, accuracy, intel-
lectual property, and access), which could be adopted
by robotics:

Privacy: What information about one’s self or one’s
associations must a person reveal to others, under
what conditions, and with what safeguards? What
things can people keep to themselves and not be
forced to reveal to others?

Accuracy: Who is responsible for the authentic-
ity, ﬁdelity, and accuracy of information? Similarly,
who is to be held accountable for errors in informa-
tion and how is the injured party to be made whole?

Property: Who owns information? What are the just
and fair prices for its exchange? Who owns the
channels, especially airways, through which infor-
mation is transmitted? How should access to this
scarce resource be allocated?

Accessibility: What information does a person or an
organization have the right or privilege to obtain,
under what conditions, and with what safeguards?
Problems of the delegation and accountability to
and within technology are daily life problems of all of
us. Today, we give responsibility for crucial aspects of
our security, health, and life-saving, and so on to ma-
chines.
Professionals are advised to apply, in perform-
ing sensitive technologies the precautionary princi-
ple [80.32]:
When an activity raises threats of harm to human
health or the environment, precautionary measures
should be taken even if some cause-and-effect rela-
tionships are not fully established scientiﬁcally.
From the precautionary principle some other rules
are derived, such as:

Non-instrumentalization

Non-discrimination

Informed consent and equity

Sense of reciprocity

Data protection.
All over the world, associations and orders of engi-
neers have adopted codes of ethics guiding to respon-
sible conduct in research and practice. In this context,
security and reliability are the most important ethical
codes of conduct.
Among the other important recommendations are
the following:

Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of
the public in the performance of their professional
duties

80.9 Legal Issues in Robotics
Because of their increasing autonomy and anthropo-
morphic characteristics, robots are inherently different
from other man-made devices and systems and hence
require the development of new legal structures under
which they operate (and will operate) in society. At
present there is no clear legal framework on which to
append issues relating to the behavior of autonomous,
intelligent robots, and what distinguishes their behav-
ior from that of human beings. Since robot intelligence
is provided by their on-board computers, they too will
require new legal frameworks. For example, about 15
years ago, Kurzweil wrote that by 2029 there will be
a growing discussion about the legal rights of com-
puters and what constitutes being human. Further, he
states that Machines will claim to be conscious and
these claims will be largely accepted [80.34]. Whether
we accept this forecast or not, it illustrates the fact
that our current legal structures have no provisions
for dealing with autonomous machines [80.35]. Fur-
ther, many of the ethical issues discussed earlier in
this chapter will require legal support for their im-
plementation, since society depends on law for the
enforcement of its ethical foundations. Some of the
major legal issues concerning robots in society in-
clude responsibility, liability, attribution, agency, and
privacy. We consider these points brieﬂy (and super-
ﬁcially) in this section. A major treatment of these
issues has been provided by Asaro [80.36, 37], Moon
and Nass [80.38], Dennett [80.39], Calo [80.40], Den-
ning [80.41], Sharkey [80.42], and others.
80.9.1 Responsibility
In the present state of the art, we can say that a dumb
or even a semi-autonomous robot that breaks the law
does so because of bad design, bad programming, or
bad construction. This implies that we need to attribute
responsibility for improper or illegal behavior to the
owners, designers, and/or builders of the machines.
The question of responsibility becomes increasingly
complex as the robots become more autonomous and
capable of modifying their behavior through learning
and experience, since their behavior will no longer be
based entirely on their original design. Of course, one
could attribute the learned behavior to the designers of
the artiﬁcial intelligence programs; a second-order at-
tribution. This is another issue for the writers of future
laws. When human beings break the law, the conse-
quences may be punishments, such as paying ﬁnes or
serving time in jail. Such punishments do not apply
to robots, unless their behavior is attributed to humans
with evil intentions, who then face the consequences.
A related issue is that of agency, a legal term im-
plying that one person acts on behalf of another; he/she
is the agent of the second person. Thus, in real estate
transactions, a salesman may be my agent and represent
me in discussions with potential buyers of my house. If
a robot can be considered an agent of a person, then the
attribution of responsibility is clear and direct. Even so,
there will be legal issues concerning the (mis)behavior
of a robot owned by Mr. A, but acting as an agent for
Mr. B. Such a situation may arise if B is a hacker and
has gained control of the robot’s computer.
80.9.2 Liability
Liability is the legal consequence of responsibility. If
my robot breaks your property, even accidentally, I am
responsible and liable. This is civil liability. If it can
be proven that my robot harmed a person as a result
of negligence on my part in the design, programming,
or fabrication of the robot, I may also be criminally li-
able. Liability is a major cause of legal action in the
United States, it provides income to many lawyers, and
is too complex to deal with comprehensively in this
chapter. However, we can say that sometimes liability
may be apportioned, partially to the designer, partially
to the manufacturer, and partially to the user, espe-
cially if the latter has modiﬁed the robot’s hardware
or software. Even toy robots like the RoboSapien (for-
merly manufactured by WowWee Toys in Hong Kong),
have spawned Websites with guidelines for hacking the
robot’s software and modifying its behavior.
80.9.3 Privacy
The right to privacy is protected by a variety of laws.
Yet, it is clear that recent developments in robotics
will challenge both law and custom in this area. We
know that drones (autonomous ﬂying vehicles) carry

Roboethics: Social and Ethical Implications
80.10 Roboethics Taxonomy
2147
Part G | 80.10
new cameras with such amazing resolution that they
can discern objects 1 m in size from an altitude of
several thousand meters [80.43]. This implies that un-
manned ﬂying vehicles could spy on citizens in their
own backyards, producing pictures that could be used
for blackmail or other illegal purposes. Even more
serious are recent developments in very small ﬂying
robots, only a few centimeters in length, that could ﬂy
in and out of windows, perch in trees or on roofs of
buildings, collecting information using vision and other
sensors, including the ability to record both sounds
and smells. The legal system is not currently equipped
for handling such methods of surveillance. There is
a still more subtle form of privacy violation, discussed
by Calo [80.40] and Denning [80.41]. Consider the
increasing variety of personal robots in our homes: vac-
uum cleaners, window washers, child companions, and
assistants to the elderly and disabled. All these ma-
chines could also be spies, especially if hacked by third
parties. Recently there was controversy in the United
States over the discovery that some manufacturers of
smart phones that include global positioning system
(GPS) sensors had programmed their machines to send
the owners’ geographic location to a company’s com-
puter. This could be interpreted as another invasion of
privacy.
It is evident from the brief summary in this section
that current and future developments in robotics will
pose greater and greater challenges to the legal systems
in many countries. We believe that it is essential for rep-
resentatives of governments, the legal profession, and
robotics designers and manufacturers to begin dialogs
on this subject now, before being forced to do so by
major accidents or intentional violation of law.
80.10 Roboethics Taxonomy
Certainly, classifying the different branches of robotics
is not an easy task. Likewise, it is a complex under-
taking to organize a matrix of ﬁeld of robotics/ethical
issues. We have tried to classify these topics accord-
ing to homogeneous ﬁelds from an applicative point
of view. Furthermore, in the present taxonomy, we
have chosen the triage process of identifying the most
evident/urgent/sensitive ethical problems in robotics,
leaving more complex problems to other times and fur-
ther studies.
80.10.1 Industrial Robotics
An industrial robot is ofﬁcially deﬁned by the Interna-
tional Standards Organization (ISO) as an automatically
controlled, reprogrammable, multipurpose manipula-
tor. Typical applications of industrial robots include
welding, painting, ironing, assembly, pick and place,
palletizing, product inspection, and testing, all accom-
plished with high endurance, speed, and precision.
Complexity can vary from a simple single robot to
very complex multi-robot systems:

Robotic arms

Robotic work cells

Assembly lines.
From the social and economic standpoint, the ben-
eﬁts of these robots are extraordinary. They can relieve
human beings of heavy work, dangerous workplaces,
and routine and tedious activities. In the future, we
can imagine robotic factories, completely managed by
robots. In industrialized countries, which are facing
looming labor shortages due to aging societies, robots
in factories will cut costs. Industrial robots increase pro-
ductivity (higher speed, better endurance); they increase
quality (precision, cleanliness, endurance); they make
highly miniaturized devices possible.
Social problems stemming from the introduction of
robots in factories are, ﬁrst of all, loss of jobs, and un-
employment. On the other hand, while a welfare policy
is to be implemented at national level to facilitate work-
ers’ reconversion, and educational programs to create
new skills, it should also be said that robots have also
created new jobs directly and can create wealth, leading
to the development of new industries and workplaces.
80.10.2 Service Robots
Service robots are robots of several shapes and sizes
(wheeled, legged, humanoids), equipped with differ-
ent kinds of sensing systems (artiﬁcial vision systems,
ultrasonic, radio) and manipulations (grippers, hands,
tools, probes). Service robots support and back up hu-
man operators. These robots represent one of the fastest
growing areas of robotics, and they raise a large num-
ber of ethical issues. According to the International
Federation of Robotics (IFR) World Robotics Report,
2014 [80.44], the total number of professional service
robots sold in 2012 went up to 6067units; likewise, IFR
projections for the period 2013–2016 forecast about
22 million units of service robots for personal use).
Consider ﬁrst the robots used for personal service.
In addition to the applications listed above, there are
a large number of research projects worldwide to ex-

Part G
Robots and Humans
pand robot use in the home. During the coming decade
many more robots will be present in our homes to as-
sist us in tasks such as housekeeping, washing, ironing
clothes, and child care. This trend to robots as co-
inhabitants in our homes began with a vacuum cleaning
robot introduced in United States in 2002. Since then
millions of these units have been sold, and other vac-
uum cleaners have been developed in Sweden, South
Korea, Japan, and other countries. The ability of ser-
vice robots to share our living spaces depends to some
extent on their communication skills and their ability to
relate to human beings. Humanoids are a special cate-
gory of service robots, which presents many different
ethical, legal and societal (ELS) aspects from other ser-
vice robots, to be dealt with separately.
80.10.3 Humanoids
One of the most ambitious aims of robotics is to design
an autonomous robot that could reach – and even sur-
pass – human intelligence and performance in partially
unknown, changing, and unpredictable environments.
Artiﬁcial intelligence will be able to lead the robot
to fulﬁll the missions required by the end-users. To
achieve this goal, over the past decades scientists have
been working on AI techniques in many ﬁelds. Among
these are:
a) Artiﬁcial vision
b) Perception and analysis of the environment
c) Natural language processing
d) Human interaction
e) Cognitive systems
f)
Machine learning, behaviors
g) Neural networks.
In this context, one of the fundamental aspects of
the robots is their capability to learn: to learn the charac-
teristics of the surrounding environment, that is, a) the
physical environment, but also b) the living beings that
inhabit it. This means that robots working in a given en-
vironment have to distinguish human beings from other
objects. In addition to learning about the environment,
robots have to learn about their own behavior, through
a self-reﬂective process. They have to learn from the
experience, replicating somehow the natural processes
of the evolution of intelligence in living beings (synthe-
sis procedures, trial-and-error, learning by doing, and
so on).
It is almost inevitable that human designers are in-
clined to replicate their own conception of intelligence
in the intelligence of robots. In turn, the former be-
comes incorporated into the control algorithm of the
robots. Robotics intelligence is a learned intelligence,
fed by the world’s models uploaded by the designers.
It is a self-developed intelligence, evolved through the
experience that robots have gained through the learned
effects of their actions. Robotics intelligence also com-
prises the ability to evaluate what attributes a judgment
to the actions carried out.
All these processes embodied in robots produce
a kind of intelligent machine endowed with the capa-
bility of expressing a certain degree of autonomy. It
follows that a robot can behave, in some situations, in
a way that is unpredictable for their human designers.
Basically, the increasing autonomy of the robots could
give rise to unpredictable and non-predictable behav-
iors. So, without necessarily imagining some science
ﬁction (sci-ﬁ) scenarios, where robots are provided with
consciousness, free will, and emotions, in a few years
we are going to be cohabiting with robots endowed
with self-knowledge and autonomy – in the engineer-
ing sense of these words.
Humanoids are robots whose body structure resem-
bles the human one. They answer an old dream of
humanity, and certainly do not spring only from ra-
tional, engineering, or utilitarian motivations, but also
from psycho-anthropological ones. Humanoids are the
expression of one of the demands of our European cul-
ture, which is that humankind was the creator of some
mechanical being in the shape of a human. In Japanese
culture, it is the demand to carefully replicate nature
in all its forms. It is a very difﬁcult and demanding
enterprise, a project of the level of the mission to the
Moon. However, precisely for its characteristic of be-
ing one of humanity’s dreams, the investments are high
and the progress speed very quick. It has been forecast
that in the not-so-distant future we will cohabit with
humanoids whose shape will be so similar to that of
human beings that it will render it possible to get mixed
up – in certain situations – with the latter. Humanoids
will assist human operators in human environments,
will replace human beings, and will cooperate with hu-
man beings in many ways.
Given the high cost and the delicacy of humanoids,
they will probably be employed in tasks and in en-
vironments where the human shape would really be
needed, that is, in all these situations where human–
robot interaction is primary, compared to any other mis-
sion – human–robot interactions in healthcare, assis-
tance with children/disabled people/elderly assistance,
baby sitting, ofﬁce clerks, museum guides, entertain-
ers, sexual robots, and so on. Or, they will be em-
ployed as testimonials for commercial products. The
special tasks humanoid robots can fulﬁll are man-
ifold. Humanoids are robots that are so adaptable
and ﬂexible that will be rapidly used in many sit-
uations and circumstances. They can assist humans
to perform very difﬁcult tasks, and behave like true

and reliable companions in many ways. Their shape,
and the sophisticated human–robot interaction, will be
very useful for situations where a human shape is
needed.
The research carried out in humanoids laboratories
over the world will have as a side effects the devel-
opment of a platform to study the human body, for
training, haptic tests and training, with extraordinary
outcomes on healthcare, education, edutainment, and so
on. Faced with an aging population, Japanese society
see humanoids robots as one way to enable people to
continue to lead an active and productive life in their
old age, without being a burden to other people.
From the point of view of the safety in the use of
humanoids, and taking into account that in the not so
far future they will be used as companions to human
beings, humanoids can raise serious problems related
to the reliability of the internal evaluation systems of
the robots, and to the unpredictability of robots’ be-
havior [80.41]. Thus, designers should guarantee the
traceability of evaluation/actions procedures, and the
identiﬁcation of robots.
Concerning safety, it should be underlined that
wrong action by humanoids can lead to dangerous sit-
uations for living beings and the environment. From
the point of view of security, this is the case where
the robot’s autonomy is controlled by ill-intentioned
people, who can modify the robot’s behavior in a dan-
gerous and fraudulent course. Because humanoids sum
up almost all the characteristics of the entire spec-
trum of robots, their use implies the emergence of
nearly all the problems that we examine below. In
particular, their introduction into human environments,
workplaces, homes, schools, hospitals, public places,
ofﬁces, and so on, will deeply and dramatically mod-
ify our society.
There is already an important and well-documented
literature on the implication of the coexistence between
human beings and humanoids. The problems range
from the replacement of human beings (economic prob-
lems, human unemployment, reliability, dependability,
and so on) to psychological problems (deviations in
human emotions, problems of attachment, disorgani-
zation in children, fears, panic, confusion between
real and artiﬁcial, feeling of subordination towards
robots [80.45]). Another set of questions arises around
the shape of the humanoids. Is it right that robots can
exhibit a personality? Is it right that robot can express
emotion? The concern expressed by psychologists is
that well before evolving to become conscious agents,
humanoids can be an extraordinary tool used to control
human beings.
Sophisticated humanoids raise a number of ethical
issues, including the following:

Loss of privacy for the human inhabitants if the
robots are permitted free access to all rooms in
a home.

Ability of the robots to recognize commands that
may lead to unethical behavior (e.g., to stealing
a neighbor’s camera or cell phone).

Rights
and
responsibilities
of
the
robots,
e.g., should they be treated with respect as if
they were human?

Emotional relationships, e.g., how should a robot re-
late to human anger, say when the robot drops a dish
of food on the ﬂoor? In other words, is it ethical to
yell at a robot? Can and should robots be punished
for misbehavior, and, if so, how?

How should a robot react to multiple instructions
from different humans, e.g., when a child calls for
it to come and play while the mother calls for it to
come and wash the dishes?

Can the robot’s computer be accessed by hackers,
so it may stake out and send pictures from the home
to potential burglars?
We believe these issues will need to be addressed
before humanoid personal service robots come into
common use.
80.10.4 Healthcare and Life Quality
Another area of service robot where robot-human in-
teraction is developing rapidly is the ﬁeld of health-
care, including nursing, surgery, physical therapy, and
non-contact assistance during therapy and rehabilita-
tion. These developments are becoming possible as
the potential danger to humans from accidental robot
activity decreases. This area of robotics is growing
so rapidly that we can only indicate some typical
applications.
From the social and ethical standpoint, this is one
of the ﬁelds in robotics that bears the most sensi-
tive safety and ethical problems. From a technical
point of view, scientists in robot-surgery are work-
ing on the problems of reduced dexterity, workspace,
and sensory input and possible fatal trouble, which
could originate from a breakdown of surgical robot
systems. Also issues of size, cost, and functionality
should be addressed in surgery and haptic and assistive
robotics.
In the context of assistive technology, some ques-
tions can be posed concerning the relationship between
patients and health structures in which they are treated.
Are we going to mechanize hospitals and to dehuman-
ize our patients? Shall we improve our health structures,
where human nurses can care about patients? Can we
not develop new psychological and physical dependen-

2150
Part G
Robots and Humans
cies? As a general principle of awareness, we should
underline that the high cost of robotic systems in the
medical ﬁeld could widen the digital divide between de-
veloped and developing countries; and between layers
of the same population.
The ﬁeld of implantations raises concerns related to
the fact that direct brain interfaces may at the same time
pose ethical questions related to the enhancement of hu-
man function.
Assistive Robots
Assistive technology will help many people to conduct
a more independent life.
Nursing care is typically a one-on-one relationship
between a patient and a caregiver. Hence, it is an ex-
pensive part of healthcare, and a number of laboratories
are developing robots that we may term nurse’s as-
sistants. One of the earliest of such robots was the
wheeled HelpMate, currently marketed by a company
named Pyxis. HelpMate assists nurses and other hos-
pital personnel by smoothly transporting pharmaceu-
ticals, laboratory specimens, equipment and supplies,
meals, medical records, and radiology ﬁlms back and
forth between support departments, nursing ﬂoors, and
patient rooms. HelpMate is able to navigate hospital
corridors, avoid collisions with humans, summon the
elevator, and locate a speciﬁc patient’s room. Carnegie
Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh have
developed a nurse-bot named Pearl [80.46] as an as-
sistant who visits elderly patients in hospital rooms,
provides information, reminds patients to take their
medication, takes messages, and guides residents. Such
robots are usually constructed as upright structures on
wheels, with a somewhat human-appearing head con-
taining cameras and voice synthesizing software for
communication. They usually also have a digital dis-
play, on the head or chest, to display messages. In
Europe, there have been (and are) a number of projects
in this area, such as the Care-o-Bot developed in 2010
at the Fraunhofer Institute in Stuttgart, Germany. The
Care-o-Bot also has an arm to assist in pick-and-place
operations. Similar projects exist in Japan, South Ko-
rea, and other countries. A different approach to robots
in healthcare involves the use of a mobile tele-presence
robot under control of remote physician, which can
travel throughout a hospital and visit patients. The
physician’s face appears on a large screen, allowing him
or her to interact with the patient. Cameras on the robot
allow the physician to see the patient, and verbal com-
munication is possible. Such robots can decrease the
need for doctors to visit patients in person, without de-
creasing the patient’s ability to interact. Such a robot,
named RP-VITA, was announced in 2012 by a joint
venture of the robotics company iRobot and InTouch
Health, a pioneer in remote presence robotics for medi-
cal applications.
A related set of projects involves assistive robots,
which provide verbal guidance, encouragement, and
interaction to people recovering from strokes, spinal in-
juries, as well as companionship to children with autism
spectrum disorders. These robots do not make any phys-
ical contact with the subjects, but rather guide them
through exercises and activities by voice and demon-
stration [80.47].
The humanoid Wakamaru, produced by Mitsubishi
in 2010 was designed to co-inhabit living spaces with
humans and was termed a companion robot for el-
derly and disabled persons. It is about 4 ft, or 120 cm,
in height, has a head with large eyes, and movable
arms but no legs; it moves on wheels, thus being re-
stricted to relatively ﬂat locations. It recognizes some
10 000 words, can place telephone calls, and commu-
nicate by internet. It carries a camera; if contacted by
internet, it displays the camera image to the caller, and
it recognizes 10 faces and can be programmed to react
appropriately to each. It can read the owner’s email and
scan the news, passing the information on by voice. It
communicates both by speech and gestures. Such robots
are provided with binocular vision, hearing, touch, and
other sensors, and can interact with humans by voice,
gesture recognition, and safe navigation in the home.
Mitsubishi originally made 100 of these robots for sale
and then provided a rental service in Japan. It has not
been available since 2012.
Among the potential ethical concerns in the use of
such assistive robots and nurse-bots are the following:

Patients may become emotionally attached to the
robots, so that any attempt to withdraw them may
cause signiﬁcant distress.

The robots will not be able to respond to patients’
anger and frustration, except by calling for human
help. For example, a patient may refuse to take the
medication offered by the robot, throw it on the
ﬂoor, and even attempt to strike the robot.

A robot may be called by more than one user and
not have the ability to prioritize the requests, thus
causing anger and frustration.
More complete discussions of these topics may be
found in the work of Bekey and Abney [80.48], and
Bekey [80.49].
Surgical Robotics
Surgical robotics allows minimally invasive surgery,
which can reduce patient recovery time. It could im-
prove accuracy and precision. Robotics system in-
creases the precision of microsurgery and enhances

Roboethics: Social and Ethical Implications

2151
Part G | 80.10
the performances of complex therapies. Surgical robots
can restore a surgeon’s dexterity. Robo-surgery is ap-
plied to very delicate neurological procedures that
are practically impossible to perform without robotic
assistance.
The ﬁeld of surgery is entering a time of great
change, spurred on by remarkable recent advances
in surgical and computer technology. Computer-
controlled diagnostic instruments have been used in the
operating theater for years to help provide vital infor-
mation through ultrasound, computer-aided tomogra-
phy (CAT), and other imaging technologies. Recently,
robotic systems have made their way into the operat-
ing room as dexterity-enhancing surgical assistants and
surgical planners, in answer to surgeons’ demands for
ways to overcome the surgical limitations of minimally
invasive laparoscopic surgery, a technique developed in
the 1980s. On July 11, 2000, FDA (Food and Drug
Administration) approved the ﬁrst completely robotic
surgery device.
Typical applications are:

Robotic telesurgical workstations

Robotic devices for endoluminal surgery

Robotic systems for diagnosis (CAT, NMR, PET)

Robots for therapy (laser eye treatment, targeted nu-
clear therapy, ultrasonic surgery)

Virtual environments for surgical training and aug-
mentation

Haptic interfaces for surgery/physiotherapy train-
ing.
Biorobotics and Biomechatronics
Biorobotics, while enhancing the quality of life after
diseases or accidents, provides tools for studying bio-
logical behavior and brain functions, and is a test bed
for the study and evaluation of biological algorithms
and modeling.
According to Dario [80.50]:
Biorobotics is a new scientiﬁc and technological
area with a unique interdisciplinary character. It
derives its methodology mainly from the sectors
of robotics and Biomedical Engineering, but also
includes knowledge from, and provides useful ap-
plications to, many sectors of engineering, basic
and applied sciences (medicine, neuroscience, eco-
nomics, law, bio/nanotechnologies in particular),
and even the humanities (philosophy, psychology,
ethics). Biorobotics offers a new paradigm for engi-
neers. The engineer no longer just cooperates with
neuroscientists, but has also become a scientist in
order to discover basic biological principles that
make their job easier.
Novel, high-performance bio-inspired machines
and systems, for many different potential applica-
tions, are being designed and fabricated. This implies
the development of (nano, micro, macro) novel de-
vices for diagnosis, surgery, prosthetics, rehabilitation
and personal assistance; and devices for biomedical
applications (e.g., mini-invasive surgery and neuro-
rehabilitation).
Biorobotics can be used for human prostheses for
locomotion, manipulation, vision, sensing, and other
functions:

Artiﬁcial limbs (legs, arms)

Artiﬁcial internal organs (heart, kidney)

Artiﬁcial senses (eye, ears, etc.)

Human augmentation (exoskeleton).
This ﬁeld has important connection with neuro-
science, to develop neural interfaces and sensory-motor
coordination systems for the integration of these bionic
devices into the human body/brain.
80.10.5 Distributed Robotic Systems
The fast growth of many wireless systems makes possi-
ble to link all robots to the Web, and among themselves.
The development of cloud systems allows control of
any addressable device, anywhere on the network, and
every device on the network can connect to one another,
creating intelligent robot groups.
Cloud, or network robotics will allow remote hu-
man–robot interaction for tele-operation and tele-pres-
ence; and, also, robot–robot interaction for data-shar-
ing and cooperative working and learning. When Web
speed will be comparable to that of the internal network
of the robot, the machine will explode into a set of spe-
cialized systems distributed over the net.
Complex robotic systems will be developed, con-
stituted by a team of co-operating robotic agents/
components connected through ICT and cloud tech-
nologies:

Networked knowledge system

Networked intelligence systems

Multi-robot systems.
Multi-robot systems are self-organizing robot teams
consisting of a large number of heterogeneous team
members. The organization in robot teams or squads is
needed to perform speciﬁc tasks that require automatic
task distribution and co-ordination at a global and local
level; and when central control becomes impossible due
to large distance and lack of local information, time of
signal traveling.

2152
Part G
Robots and Humans
A full-scale ecological robot team will be of tremen-
dous value in a number of applications such as security,
surveillance, monitoring, gardening, and pharmaceu-
tical manufacturing. In addition, the co-ordination of
heterogeneous teams of robots will also be of signiﬁ-
cant value in terms of planning, co-ordination, and use
of advanced manufacturing systems. The beneﬁts of the
robot teams are manifold; e.g., an increase in the efﬁ-
ciency of the performance of complex tasks and in the
capability to manage large-scale applications. They pro-
vide abundant and replaceable, interchangeable agents
and they raise the reliability of the robots, because the
group can perform even after losing most of its parts.
On the other hand, scientists should be aware of
some of the risks in applying robot teams, for in-
stance the increasing dependability of primary services
on complex systems, and the unpredictability of robot
team behavior. From a criminal point of view, the risks
include the assignment of liability for misbehavior or
crimes, vulnerability to hackers, and concerns about
privacy.
80.10.6 Outdoor Robotics
Outdoor robots are intelligent machines that explore,
develop, secure, and feed our world and worlds beyond
land. Robots could be employed in dangerous oper-
ations, such as laying explosives, going underground
after blasting to stabilize a mine roof, and mining in
areas where it is impossible for humans to work or even
survive.
They can work in the following environments:

Land:
–
Mining
(automated
load-haul-dump
trucks,
robotic drilling and blasting devices)
–
Cargo handling (cranes and other automation
technology for cargo lift on/lift off)
–
Agricultural (autonomous tractors, planters and
harvesters, applicators for fertilizers and pest
control)
–
Road vehicles (autonomous vehicles for humans
or cargo transportation)
–
Rescue robotics (robots that support ﬁrst re-
sponse units in disaster missions)
–
Humanitarian demining (robots for detecting,
localizing and neutralizing land mines)
–
Environmental protection (robots for pollution
cleaning and decommissioning of dangerous
plants).

Sea:
–
Research (marine robots for oceanography, ma-
rine biology, geology)
–
Offshore (underwater robots for inspection,
maintenance, repair and monitoring of oil and
gas facilities in deep and ultra deep waters)
–
Search and rescue (underwater robots for ﬁrst
response intervention in casualties at sea, like
submarines run aground).

Air:
–
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) (autonomous
airplanes for weather forecasting, environmen-
tal monitoring, road trafﬁc control, large area
survey, patrolling).

Space:
–
Space exploration (deep space vehicles, landing
modules, rovers)
–
Space stations (autonomous laboratories, con-
trol and communication facilities)
–
Remote operation (autonomous or supervised
dexterous arms and manipulators).
Mobile robots in particular can be highly valuable
tools in urban rescue missions after catastrophes like
earthquakes, bomb or gas-explosions, or everyday inci-
dents like ﬁres and road accidents involving hazardous
materials. Robots can be used to inspect collapsed
structures, to assess the situation, and to search and lo-
cate victims). Among the beneﬁts of employing such
robots is a rise in the efﬁciency of the exploitation of
natural resources, to increase food production for the
world population.
Concerning space robotics, it is obvious that, on the
basis of current knowledge and technology, the robot
can be our pioneer in space travels and mission of ex-
ploration of the far planets of the solar system and
beyond.
On the social front, the unrestrained and planned
use of outdoor robots can extend to its limit the ex-
cessive anthropization and exploitation of the planet,
which can, in turn, become a threat to biodiversity and
all the other forms of life on the planet. As for all
other branches of robotics, this could lead to technology
addiction. Furthermore, given the versatility of these
robots, they can also be used the wrong way round,
when reconverted from civilian use to devices for war-
fare and misuses (terrorism, pollution).
80.10.7 Military Robotics
After numerous science ﬁction stories about war-ﬁght-
ing robots during the twentieth century (and earlier), the
stories have become reality in the twenty-ﬁrst century.
While military robots are now used extensively by the
United States, a number of other countries are also de-
veloping robot weapons and, unfortunately, the world

Roboethics: Social and Ethical Implications
80.10 Roboethics Taxonomy
2153
Part G | 80.10
has yet to come to terms with the ethical issues that arise
from the use of such systems.
Humanity has been involved in war from the earliest
days of homo sapiens on Earth. A famous psychologist
published a book a few years ago entitled The Terri-
ble Love of War [80.51]; this title summarizes the issue.
The love of war has resulted in a love of weapons,
as efﬁcient ways to kill the enemy. Further, much of
the development of weapons has been devoted to ﬁnd-
ing ways of inﬂicting death at a distance, to avoid
injury to the attacker. Attacking an enemy with a club
allows the victim to strike back, but attacking with
bows and arrows allows the attacker to kill at a dis-
tance. Clearly, the development of muskets and guns
allowed for greater and greater distances. This trend
continues with military robots. Today there are many
categories of robot vehicles equipped with weapons.
Each of these systems can be controlled from a dis-
tance, allowing the owners of the vehicles to stay out
of danger.

Intelligent weapons: This ﬁeld comprises all de-
vices resulting from the development of traditional
systems by robotics technology (automation, artiﬁ-
cial intelligence, etc.):
–
Integrated defense systems: AI systems for in-
telligence and surveillance controlling weapons
and aircraft capabilities
–
Unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs): autono-
mous tanks, armored vehicles carrying weapons
and/or tactical payloads
–
Intelligent bombs and missiles
–
UAVs: also referred to as autonomous ﬂying
vehicles (AFVs). Unmanned spy planes and re-
motely piloted bombers
–
AUVs (autonomous underwater vehicles): intel-
ligent torpedoes and autonomous submarines

Robot soldiers: Eventually humanoids may be em-
ployed to substitute humans in performing sensitive
tasks and missions in environments populated by
humans. The main reasons for using humanoids are
to permit a one-by-one substitution, without mod-
ifying the environment, or the engagement rules.
This could be required where a safeguard of hu-
man life is considered a priority in many different
scenarios:
–
Urban terrain combat
–
Indoor security operations
–
Patrol
–
Surveillance.
Outdoor security robots could be able to make their
night watch rounds and even chase criminals, di-
rected by a remote control system via an internet
connection or moving autonomously via their own
artiﬁcial intelligence systems.

Superhuman: There are several projects aimed at
developing a superhuman soldier. Actually, the hu-
man body cannot perform tasks with the strength,
speed, and fatigue resistance of the machines. Aug-
mentation indicates the possibility of extending hu-
man’s existing capabilities through wearable robot
exoskeletons, to create superhuman strength, speed,
and endurance:
–
Artiﬁcial sensor systems
–
Augmented reality
–
Exoskeletons.
Drones
Among the most visible of robotic vehicles capa-
ble of lethal force are semi-autonomous ﬂying robots
equipped with guided missiles, which are capable of
ﬂying over long distances to targets identiﬁed by GPS
coordinates. These vehicles are known as autonomous
combat ﬂying vehicles (ACFVs), or more commonly
as drones. While such vehicles are autonomous robots
as far as ﬂying is concerned (including takeoff and
landing), they can ﬁre lethal weapons only by human
command. Drones ﬂying over Afghanistan or various
targets in Africa are controlled from Creech Air Force
Base (near Las Vegas), or a base in New Mexico, thou-
sands of kilometers away from the vehicles themselves.
The drone carries extremely high-resolution cameras;
the images are transmitted to the human controllers who
can steer the aircraft so that a target is within the cross
hairs of the on-board missiles. Human controllers acti-
vate and release the weapons. In the USA at the present
time no ﬂying robot is given the autonomy needed to re-
lease weapons without human supervision. Early 2013,
there were an estimated 7500 drones in the US military
arsenal, many ﬂown in secret missions by the Central
Intelligence Agency.
Drones (and other robot vehicles on land or under
water) have been discussed in detail in recent books
and other publications. Among the most inﬂuential au-
thors are Sharkey, Singer, and Arkin. Sharkey from the
University of Shefﬁeld in the UK is a proliﬁc writer on
the subject [80.42, 52–54]. Singer, a researcher at the
Brookings Institution in Washington, DC is a proliﬁc
author and has published a highly inﬂuential book en-
titled Wired for War [80.43]. Arkin from the Georgia
Institute of Technology worked under a US Army con-
tract to develop an ethical governor for killer robots,
to be included in their software system [80.55]. A very
complete description of military robots can be found
in the book by Ramo entitled Let Robots Do the Dy-
ing [80.56]. While 10 years ago the USA was the

Part G | 80.10
2154
Part G
Robots and Humans
only country possessing autonomous ﬂying vehicles,
in 2012 it was estimated that 70 countries have AFV
programs, but only about 15 of these have military
drones.
The ethical issues arising from the use of drones in-
clude the following:

Unintended injury or death of innocent non-combat-
ants (usually known as collateral damage). While
the missiles launched by a drone are extremely pre-
cise in steering to their intended targets, nearby
civilians are frequently killed as well.

The very fact that the human controllers who re-
lease the weapons are very far away, so that they
do not see the blood and destruction directly but
only from the drone’s cameras means that for some
of them such activities are more like a video game
rather than the killing and destruction of human
beings.

Drones are used to attack suspected terrorists in
countries that (ofﬁcially) are not at war. Hence, they
are used in undeclared wars. This may be a violation
of international law, and it certainly raises ethical
issues. It has been suggested that the availability of
such military robots could make it easier for a coun-
try to start a war, since its own citizens would not be
in danger.
Other Military Robots
Robot vehicles known as Packbots have been used in
Iraq and Afghanistan for nearly a decade to locate and
destroy improvised explosive devices (IEDs). Prior to
the development and deployment of these robots (man-
ufactured by iRobot, Inc. in the USA), IEDs hidden in
bushes and behind rocks were the major cause of US
soldier casualties in Iraq. Now, these small tank-like ve-
hicles that can be carried by a soldier in a backpack are
able to locate and destroy the mines.
Robots are currently being used as mules to assist
soldiers in carrying heavy equipment, e.g., Big Dog,
a four-legged robot built by Boston Dynamics to carry
heavy weights over rough terrain [80.57]. The military
also have robots designed to retrieve a wounded soldier
and carry him or her to a safe location for medical help,
and a variety of other special-purpose robots. Finally,
there are programs in the USA and in Japan to provide
an exoskeleton for a human soldier, enabling him or her
to carry much larger loads than would be possible with-
out assistance.
In conclusion. The beneﬁts of military robots are as
follows:
a) Tactical/operational strength superiority
b) Unemotional behavior
c) Limited loss of human lives in the robotized army
d) Better performances of superhuman versus human
soldier.
Problems could arise from the following:
a) The inadequacy to manage the unstructured com-
plexity of a hostile scenario
b) The unpredictability of machine behavior
c) The assignment of liability for misbehavior or
crimes
d) The increased risk of starting a video game-like war,
due to the decreased perception of its deadly effects.
Humans in mixed teams could face practical and
psychological problems in having to distinguish hu-
mans from robots. Superhuman soldiers could also
tackle problems of overstress and de-humanization.
It is clear that military robots are here and they have
changed the nature of warfare dramatically. However,
there are currently no international treaties or agree-
ments governing their use, which raises serious ethical
questions. The growing deployment of military robots
(drones, mobile robots, exoskeletons) in many war the-
aters, and especially in the war on terrorism has caused
the birth of a movement devoted to stopping killing
robots. Likewise, some roboticists have ﬁrmly opposed
the fact that autonomous robots have the license to kill
humans because, in their judgment, the responsibility
of a human life should always fall on another human
being [80.58]. Military robotics should be thoroughly
examined by specialized international organizations, as
is the case with every type of military technology, to be
regulated by international conventions or agreements.
80.10.8 Educational Robot Kits
The beneﬁcial applications of robotics in education
are known and documented. Robotics is a very good
tool for teaching technology (and many other subjects)
whilst, at the same time, always remaining very tightly
anchored to reality. Robots are real, three-dimensional
(3-D) objects that move in space and time, and can em-
ulate human/animal behavior; but, unlike video games,
they are real machines, true objects, and students learn
much more quickly and easily if they can interact with
concrete objects as opposed to formulas and abstract
ideas.
In the age of electronics, computers and networks,
it is necessary to modernize not only the contents and
tools, but also the educational methods of traditional
schools. It is also important to consider that the lifestyle
of young people has changed, as well as the communi-
cation tools they use in their free time. Today, young

2155
Part G | 80.10
people communicate via the Internet and mobile tele-
phones using e-mail, sms, and chat rooms, which allow
them to be continually connected to a global commu-
nity that has no limits regarding location and time.
Young people spend more time playing video
games, playing with mobile phones, or downloading
ﬁles from the Internet. These activities provide them
with experiences, which are by now at the same stan-
dard as the most sophisticated technological systems.
All this has accelerated the pace of life, so much so
that fruition and consumption of experiences are both
real and virtual. In fact, we are entering the age of
cyberspace, which will not replace normal life relation-
ships, but will certainly alter their characteristics.
In this context, we need to consider that traditional
teaching and classical tools of support (books, doc-
umentaries) are at risk of becoming unsuitable when
compared with the everyday possibilities offered to
these young people by the world of mass media.
Therefore, it is necessary begin to plan new ways to
transmit knowledge which exploit the potential of new
technology.
Learning about robotics is important not only for
those students who want to become robotics engineers
and scientists, but for every student, because this pro-
vides a strong method of reasoning and a powerful
tool for grappling with the world. Robotics collects all
the competencies needed for designing and construct-
ing machines (mechanics, electrotechnics, electronics),
computers, software, systems of communications, and
networks. The special features of robotics boost stu-
dent creativity, communication skills, cooperation, and
teamwork. Learning about robotics promotes students’
interest in and commitment to traditional basic dis-
ciplines (math, physics, technical drawing). Robotic
construction kits, conjugating the physical building of
artifacts with their programming, can foster the devel-
opment of new ways of thinking that encourage new
reﬂections on the relationship between the following:
a) Life and technology
b) Science and its experimental tool set
c) Robot design and values and identity [80.59].
80.10.9 Entertainment Robotics and Art
Entertaining robots are already used in featuring and ad-
vertising corporate logos, products, and events. These
are marketing tools shown off by manufacturers on
special occasions. Robot toys fall into the same cat-
egory. They can be speciﬁcally designed to stimulate
children’s creativity and the development of their in-
tellectual faculties. They can become children’s com-
panions, and – for the only child – could play the role
of friends, brothers, or the traditional imaginary ﬁend.
They could be used in the pedagogical assistance of
autistic children.
On the negative side of technology, robot toys could
cause psychological problems, such as:

Lost touch with the real world

Confusion between natural and artiﬁcial

Confusion between real and imaginary

Technology addiction.
Other entertainment robots will enable building real
environments, which could be either perfect (or scaled)
copies of some of existing environments, or reconstruc-
tions of settings that existed centuries/millennia ago,
and which we can be populated by real or imaginary an-
imals. Robots and robotics settings will make it possible
to build up natural phenomena and biological processes,
even cruel ones, but without involving living beings.
In these settings, the users/audience could live interac-
tive experiences, which are real, not only virtual. As
extraordinary theatrical machines, robots will develop
ever more realistic special effects.
In this frame, we should also consider sexual robots.
These robots will be an important market ﬁeld. They are
used as sexual partners in many ﬁelds, from therapy to
prostitution from the social standpoint. Some authors
have proposed that their use could decrease the sexual
exploitation of women and children [80.60]. They could
also raise problems related to intimacy/attachments and
safety and reliability.
The role of robotics in contemporary art, along
with all the interactive artistic expressions (telecommu-
nications, and interactive installations), is gaining im-
portance and success. Artists are employing advanced
technologies to create environments and works of art,
utilizing the actuators and sensors to allow their robots
to react and change in relation to viewers.
Robotic art will spread because of the following:

It recalls (and is inspired by) the mythological tra-
ditions of various cultures. These traditions have
created fantastic synthetic creatures.

Robots exert a special fascination on the population
at large.

Robots can be used as tools in artwork and enable
the building of artistic expression in shorter times,
thus expanding the borders of human creativity.

Robots can also perform actor’s rules and allow
playing living art.
The social and individual problems that can be
produced by robotic art are, on the one hand, the dis-
semination of misinformation (wrong information on
technology can be spread through art). On the other
hand, technology can prevail over creativity.

80.11 Roboethics Enforced: From Ideals to Rules
At the conclusion of our taxonomy, and having ana-
lyzed the ethical issues in robotics outlining the main
roboethics principles, we have to ask ourselves how
roboethics conception and vision could become laws,
rules, and standards. This question is more general:
How have ethical principles been incorporated into
laws and right, after having been discussed in trans-
disciplinary assemblies, expressed by warnings or the
public’s concern, suggested by religious personalities,
theologians, and moral leaders, and/or forwarded by
a community of concerned scientists? How is ethical
thrust embodied in the R&D activity without imposing
on it unjustiﬁed restrictions, so depriving the scientist
of his/her own freedom of thought?
Along millennia of the history of science and tech-
nology, society has envisaged ways to express their
ethical concern. These include the following. The pro-
fessional oath is either a statement or a promise ex-
pressed by a new entry in professional careers to be
faithful to the traditional values of the professional or-
der he/she is entering into. The ancient Hippocratic
oath is the recurrent example for other initiatives to
develop and implement codes of conduct for scien-
tists in general, and scientists in speciﬁc areas in
particular.
A manifesto is a public declaration of intentions,
opinions, objectives, or motives, often issued by a pri-
vate organization or a government. For example, the
Russell–Einstein Manifesto of 1955 is a public dec-
laration against war and the further development of
weapons of mass destruction.
A statement or a declaration can be employed to un-
derline a given topic. As such, it can be either weakly
or strongly prescriptive, morally or legally binding. For
instance, during the World Robot Conference which
took place in Fukuoka, Japan, the participants released
a three-part list of expectations for next-generation
robots, called the World Robot Declaration issued on
February 25, 2004. It states that:

Next-generation robots will be partners that coexist
with human beings.

Next-generation robots will assist human beings
both physically and psychologically.

Next-generation robots will contribute to the real-
ization of a safe and peaceful society.
A recommendation serves to induce acceptance or
favor. It is a prescription only in the weak sense of offer-
ing advice; a normative suggestion that is neither legally
nor morally binding. More conclusive is the appeal, an
earnest request for support: a petition, entreaty, or plea.
A resolution is a formal expression of opinion or
intention made (usually after voting) by a formal orga-
nization, legislature, or other group.
In the last 50 years, many professional associations
have adopted their code, a written text that offers a col-
lection of laws, regulations, guidelines, rules, directives
or principles for moral conduct. The guiding princi-
ples of the code of research ethics are non-malfeasance
and beneﬁcence, indicating a systematic regard for the
rights and interests of others in the full range of aca-
demic relationships and activities. Non-malfeasance is
the principle of doing, or permitting, no ofﬁcial miscon-
duct. It is the principle of doing no harm in the widest
sense. Beneﬁcence is the requirement to serve the in-
terests and well-being of others, including respect for
their rights. It is the principle of doing well in the widest
sense.
The charter is an ancient form of agreement. An ex-
ample is the Charter of the United Nations. The charters
have a legal character and are connected, in principle,
to sanctions when not properly executed. Other means
of implementing ethical concerns in science and tech-
nology are the convention, a form of agreement, or
a contract, and also a practice established by general
consent.
From a technical point of view, to ensure that robot
and robotics devices adhere to the established applied
ethical principles, standards have to be established.
Generally, these standards are the results of the work of
professional committees, which are expressed by pro-
fessional and control bodies. At national level there are
committees like ANSI (USA) or DIN (Germany). At the
international level, ISO. Inside ISO is working a com-
mitted devoted to establishing technical standards for
industrial and service robotics (TC184/SC2 robots and
robotic devices). This committee is organized in several
sub-committee groups: WG1 vocabulary to compile
terms and deﬁnitions from all standards dealing with
robots, WG3 industrial safety for the assurance of
safety in design and construction of the robot and for
the safeguarding of personnel during robot operations,
WG 7 personal care safety on the development of safety
standards for personal care robots, and WG 8 service
robots on the development of safety standards for ser-
vice robots.
Finally, in order that all previous instances and
applied ethical principles be enforceable, they should
become national laws. Each national government must
incorporate those principles and standards in their own
legislation, developing the required technical standards
of implementations, and setting up adequate rules for
violations.

Roboethics: Social and Ethical Implications
80.12 Conclusions and Further Reading
2157
Part G | 80.12
80.12 Conclusions and Further Reading
We are witnessing a true, growing interest in robots in
the general public, who are often more excited than the
insiders, whose feelings swing between a position of
cultural indifference to a behavior dictated by external
pressures, be they political or industrial. We are also
noticing the modern change – which already happened
in the 1970s in the ﬁeld of computer science – of the
transformation of the robot from a research platform
and a working tool to a consumer goods and an object
of entertainment. It is a juvenile phenomenon, as shown
by the increase of robotics contests among high school
students. Today’s young people who are getting their
hands in the robotics kits will be the robotics profes-
sionals and the consumers of tomorrow.
A growing interest about the social effects of
robotics is easy to observe among international pro-
fessional associations and orders, stretching over the
sister ﬁelds of computer ethics and bioethics. Certainly,
roboethics is still far from being a well-established ap-
plied ethics, and by well-established we mean it has
acquitted two qualities: on the one hand, roboethics
should be universally accepted and standardized – or,
at least, adopted by some communities, relevant in
size and in political/economic/cultural inﬂuence. On the
other, it should be embodied in the practice of the de-
sign, production and use of robots.
In fact, considering the history of the two widely ap-
plied and structured ethics which are extensively stud-
ied and which reach a certain organic unity, bioethics
and computer and information ethics [80.61], we ac-
knowledge that their development, which has been
happening for over 30 years, came about with leaps
and contradictions, chasms, and bends, and that they
are far from being a suitable ethical standard shared
by a plurality of subjects. Both these ethics were born
in a policy and legislative vacuum, as technological
changes have outpaced ethical developments, bringing
about unanticipated problems [80.16].
The standardization of roboethics requires the ac-
complishment of some fundamental steps, both cultur-
ally and institutionally. From the general standpoint, it
demands that the application of robotics to the human
environment, especially to sensitive areas of human life,
will be accepted by the quasi-totality of cultures, as has
happened with other techno-scientiﬁc innovations such
as electricity and computer systems. (In the case of free
access to the Internet, the issue is still questionable in
many of the world’s nations.)
Should such a level be achieved, roboethics would
have already passed the phase of being adjusted to
ﬁt different answers and situations, to being modi-
ﬁed to the point of having acquired the capability of
adapting to the different points of views. Different cul-
tures and religions regard the intervention in sensitive
ﬁelds like human reproduction, neural therapies, im-
plantations, and privacy differently. These differences
originate from the cultural speciﬁcities regarding funda-
mental issues. For example, the limit between a human
and a cyborg, the separation between the natural and
the artiﬁcial [80.62], the difference between human and
artiﬁcial intelligence, the border between privacy and
traceability of actions, the concept of integrity and the
unity of the human being, the acceptance of diversity
(in gender, ethnicity, minorities, etc.), the boundary be-
tween replacement and human enhancement, and so
on. These are all milestones in deﬁning the underlying
paradigms, which, in turn, inﬂuence the day-by-day be-
havior of everyone.
From the experience provided by more than 30
years of discussions and disputes in the ﬁelds of
bioethics and information ethics, we know that none of
the achievements in the ﬁeld of science and ethics are
easy or negligible. For those who wish to thoroughly
investigate some elements of the philosophy of science,
the history of science and ethics, science and engineer-
ing ethics, the law applied to science and technology,
we now suggest some fundamental steps.
In the ﬁeld of the moral theories related to science
and technology, we mention the considerable work of
Beauchamp of the Kennedy Institute of Ethics [80.63]
and of Jasanoff at Harvard University Program on
Science and Technology Studies [80.64]. Two impor-
tant annual gatherings of computer philosophy, CEPE
(Computer Ethics Philosophical Enquiry) and IACAP
(International Association for Computing and Philoso-
phy) have recently added roboethics as one of their key
topics.
Furthermore, it is very useful to follow the activity
of the regulatory bodies entitled to deal with the issues
of science and ethics. In accordance with what was said
in Sects. 80.6–80.8 of this chapter, the person’s inter-
est should start from the general principles which are
essentially accepted by most of the world’s nations (at
least nominally), and come down to the speciﬁc appli-
cations in our ﬁeld.
The issue of the inﬂuence and the pressure given by
the market on science and on R&D is handled by the
applied ethics is called business ethics. In this frame,
corporate social responsibility is one of the ways in
which enterprises can afﬁrm ethical principles and val-
ues. This state of view was introduced to the USA 15
years ago (especially in the ﬁeld of healthcare) and
is still running today. Also, training in the responsi-
ble conduct of research (RCR) has been adopted by the

Part G | 80.12
2158
Part G
Robots and Humans
USA, and is still continuing in the present time. The do-
main of RCR training does not include solely the ethical
dimensions of research with human subjects, but every
intricate dimension of responsible conduct in the plan-
ning, performance, analysis, and reporting of research.
Difﬁculties here arise from the small amounts of re-
sources allocated. See also the ethical paragraphs of the
OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and
Development) guidelines for multinational enterprises.
Concerning the philosophical and epistemological
aspect of the issue in ethics and robotics, one of
the main problems that people who are interested in
roboethics will have to handle is the persistent con-
fusion – ontologically, but especially linguistically –
between human and artiﬁcial intelligence, as well as be-
tween other fundamental concepts of perception, con-
sciousness, self-consciousness, emotions, and so on, as
applied to humans and machines. It must be clariﬁed
that actual contemporary roboethics is human ethics as
applied to robotics, which is considered non-human.
A strong base of human roboethics is needed in order
to construct the foundations to knowing how to respon-
sibly manage the ﬁnal problem, the one which, so far,
no-one knows how to answer: can robots ever become
humans [80.65]?
The need for serious and thorough work on the
concepts of intelligence, knowledge, conscience, auton-
omy, freedom, free will, etc., is highlighted. Indeed, the
heterogeneous composition of specialists often leads
to incessant discussions about the meaning of words,
rather than on the contents of the myriad of, often press-
ing, issues that need to be faced.
From all this, the necessity that the international
community of robotics becomes the author of its own
destiny is born, so as to directly face the task that
needs deﬁning, whilst collaborating with academics in
the ﬁeld of philosophy, of law, and generally experts of
human sciences, the ethics and social aspects of their
researches and applications of the former. Nor should
they feel relegated to a merely techno-scientiﬁc role,
delegating to others the task of reﬂecting and taking
action on moral aspects. On the other hand, a closed-
shop attitude would be damaging to the development
of robotics, given the interdisciplinary nature of the
amount of research undertaken in the ﬁeld of robotics.
From this point of view, roboethics cannot fail to
be beneﬁcial to robotics, framing the research in close
connection with the end-users and society, so avoiding
many problems that other sensitive ﬁelds are now fac-
ing. All this, and more, will be wishful thinking if in
the engineers’ curriculum of study subjects such as: sci-
entiﬁc philosophy, history of science, law and politics
of science (as is already happening in some advanced
polytechnics) are not included. Once again, we have to
say that the deeper study into the history of science,
for example, especially in the 1800s and 1900s, cannot
but aid a better understanding of that complex scientiﬁc
galaxy which is robotics. Even a restricted knowledge
of cybernetics and of computer science, from Wiener, to
von Neumann, to Weizenbaum, will immediately and
directly demonstrate that these scientists immediately
took care of ethical and social aspects of their discover-
ies and realizations, which marked the beginning of the
ﬁeld of computers and robotics.
As an example – in 2012 some young engineers
started a project called the Open Roboethics Initiative
(ORI) [80.66]. In their words:
Open Roboethics is the idea that, just like how the
Web has allowed us to produce and maintain con-
tents of Wikipedia and software designs of Linux
by means of mass collaboration, maybe roboethics
discussions and robot designs can beneﬁt from the
power of mass collaboration.
They are creating a central Web space where pol-
icy makers, engineers/designers, and users and other
stakeholders of the technology can freely share and
access roboethics related contents; by this, they hope
to accelerate roboethics discussions and inform robot
designs.
At the same time, it is necessary that those not in-
volved in robotics keep up to date on the ﬁeld’s real
and scientiﬁcally predictable developments, in order to
base the discussions on data supported by technical and
scientiﬁc reality, and not on appearances or emotions
generated by science ﬁction. In particular, apart from,
obviously, this handbook, one must look to serious
magazines published by recognized scientiﬁc associa-
tions, and not rely on headlines about ambiguous and
scandalizing creations, which do not exist.
Ethics is a thousand-year old human science with an
impressive literature. Its application to the ﬁeld of sci-
ence technology is no doubt more recent, even though
precedents such as the Hippocratic oath suggest an
extremely ancient origin. The research on robotics is
casting light on a manifold of issues across science
and humanities. It is no wonder that it will open new
and unexpected ﬁeld of studies and application also in
ethics.
